entry.title: No Event Mesh? No Problem — Integrating Service Orders to FSM via CPI Polling
entry.content:
SAP Field Service Management (FSM) relies on timely and accurate service order data from SAP S/4HANA Cloud to dispatch technicians, schedule work, and close jobs efficiently. The standard integration between these two systems leverages SAP Event Mesh — a powerful, cloud-native messaging backbone on SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) — to stream real-time service order lifecycle events into FSM.

However, not every customer has an active SAP Event Mesh subscription on BTP. This could be due to licensing constraints, cost considerations, or an IT strategy that minimises the number of BTP service subscriptions. For these customers, the standard event-driven integration path hits a wall before it even starts.

In this blog, I will walk through a practical workaround: a custom SAP Cloud Platform Integration (CPI) polling iFlow that periodically queries the S/4HANA Cloud Service Order OData API, formats the result as a synthetic Event Mesh payload, and hands it off to the standard "Replicate Service Order from SAP S/4HANA Cloud to SAP FSM" iFlow — no Event Mesh subscription required.

Note: This work will have some limitations and considersations before adopting.

How the Standard Integration Works

The standard SAP-delivered integration uses communication arrangement SAP_COM_0092 on the S/4HANA Cloud side to publish business events to SAP Event Mesh. A subscriber iFlow on CPI then picks up those events and replicates the affected service orders into FSM.

The four events subscribed to in the standard scenario are:

  • sap/s4/beh/serviceorder/v1/ServiceOrder/Released/v1
  • sap/s4/beh/serviceorder/v1/ServiceOrder/Completed/v1
  • sap/s4/beh/serviceorder/v1/ServiceOrder/ReleaseRevoked/v1
  • sap/s4/beh/serviceorder/v1/ServiceOrder/ChgdWhenReleased/v1

Each event carries a minimal payload (service order ID, UUID, type, and description). The CPI iFlow then fetches the full service order details and pushes them into FSM. This architecture is clean, near-real-time, and fully supported by SAP — but it has one hard prerequisite: SAP Event Mesh must be provisioned and configured on BTP.

The Challenge: Event Mesh as a Hard Prerequisite

For customers who have already established an S/4HANA Cloud-to-FSM integration but do not have an Event Mesh subscription, the above architecture creates a blocking dependency. Specifically:

  1. SAP Event Mesh is a paid, separately subscribed BTP service. Customers who have not planned for it may not have it available.
  2. Activating Event Mesh mid-project introduces procurement, provisioning, and configuration lead time — often weeks — that can delay go-live.
  3. Some customers deliberately keep their BTP footprint minimal. Adding Event Mesh solely for service order integration conflicts with their platform governance model.
  4. In brownfield or upgrade scenarios, re-configuring communication arrangements and queue subscriptions can introduce regression risk to existing integrations.

These constraints call for an alternative approach — one that achieves the same functional outcome (service order replication into FSM) without any dependency on SAP Event Mesh.

Workaround approach: CPI Polling iFlow

The workaround introduces a lightweight custom polling iFlow in CPI that mimics the role of SAP Event Mesh — without actually using it. The iFlow runs on a scheduled timer (for example, every 10 minutes), queries the S/4HANA Cloud Service Order OData API for records changed since the last run, constructs a synthetic Event Mesh-style JSON payload for each changed order, and invokes the standard "Replicate Service Order" iFlow via HTTPS — exactly as if the message had arrived from Event Mesh.

Crucially, the standard iFlow is left completely untouched. This ensures SAP support scope is preserved and future upgrades to the standard content remain non-breaking.

Layer

Component

Remark

Source

S/4HANA Cloud – API_SERVICE_ORDER_SRV OData API

Standard API, no change needed

Custom iFlow

CPI Polling iFlow (customer-built)

Scheduled every ~10 min

Payload Builder

Constructs synthetic EMS JSON message

Mimics Event Mesh envelope

Target

Standard CPI iFlow – Replicate Service Order

Called via HTTPS, unmodified

Destination

SAP FSM

Unchanged end target

 

Step 1: Querying Changed Service Orders

The polling iFlow calls the standard OData API below, substituting the timestamp from the last successful run (stored as a CPI local variable):

GET /sap/opu/odata/sap/API_SERVICE_ORDER_SRV/A_ServiceOrder
  ?$select=ServiceOrder,ServiceObjectType,ServiceOrderUUID,ServiceOrderDescription,ServiceOrderType,ServiceDocChangedDateTime,ServiceOrderIsReleased,ServiceOrderIsCompleted,ServiceOrderIsRejected
  &$filter=(
    ServiceDocChangedDateTime gt datetimeoffset'<LAST_RUN_TIMESTAMP>'
    and (ServiceOrderType eq 'SVO1' or ServiceOrderType eq 'SVO2'
         or ServiceOrderType eq 'RPO1' or ServiceOrderType eq 'RPO2')
    and (ServiceOrderIsReleased eq 'X'
         or ServiceOrderIsCompleted eq 'X'
         or ServiceOrderIsRejected eq 'X')
  )

The filter targets only the service order types that are relevant for FSM replication (SVO1, SVO2, RPO1, RPO2) and only records that are in a terminal or active business state (Released, Completed, or Rejected). This keeps the result set lean and avoids processing draft or in-progress orders that FSM does not yet need.

The last-run timestamp is read from a CPI local variable at the start of each execution and updated to the current timestamp at the end of a successful run. This creates a sliding window of changes and avoids re-processing already-replicated orders.

Step 2: Splitting and Iterating

The OData response may return multiple service orders in a single call. The iFlow uses a Splitter step to process each service order independently. This is important because:

  • A failure for one service order does not block replication of others.
  • Error handling and retry logic can be applied at the individual record level.
  • The standard iFlow expects a single service order event per invocation, matching the one-event-per-message model of SAP Event Mesh.

Step 3: Constructing the Synthetic Event Mesh Payload

For each service order, the iFlow builds a JSON payload that is structurally identical to what the standard iFlow would receive from SAP Event Mesh. The event type in the payload is determined by the status flags returned by the OData API:

  • ServiceOrderIsReleased = 'X'  →  event type: ServiceOrder.Released.v1
  • ServiceOrderIsCompleted = 'X'  →  event type: ServiceOrder.Completed.v1
  • ServiceOrderIsRejected = 'X'  →  event type: ServiceOrder.ReleaseRevoked.v1

A sample constructed payload looks like this:

{
  "type": "sap.s4.beh.serviceorder.v1.ServiceOrder.Released.v1",
  "specversion": "1.0",
  "source": "/default/sap.s4.beh/0LEUVB6",
  "id": "42010aef-4c3b-1fe1-8eaa-82de726150ac",
  "time": "2026-04-16T05:21:15Z",
  "datacontenttype": "application/json",
  "data": {
    "ServiceOrder": "8000000176",
    "CustMgmtObjectType": "BUS2000116",
    "ServiceOrderUUID": "42010aef-4c8d-1fd1-8de5-b5128633bb6f",
    "ServiceOrderDescription": "Annual maintenance visit",
    "ServiceOrderType": "SVO1"
  }
}

The id field can be populated using the ServiceOrderUUID, and the time field is set to the current execution timestamp. The source field should match the BTP source identifier configured in the target standard iFlow — check the iFlow's configuration parameters to confirm the correct value.

Step 4: Invoking the Standard iFlow via HTTPS

Rather than using a ProcessDirect channel (which would require modifying the standard iFlow to expose an internal endpoint), the custom iFlow calls the standard iFlow's public HTTPS endpoint. The technical user performing this call must be assigned the WorkspaceArtifactsDeploy role in CPI to have permission to trigger iFlow executions.

This design keeps a clean boundary: the standard iFlow remains a black box from the custom iFlow's perspective. If SAP updates the standard content in a future release, no changes are needed in the custom polling iFlow as long as the input message contract (the EMS JSON structure) remains stable.

Here is a crisp, highly structured version of your content, optimized for quick scanning and professional review.

⚠️ Limitations & Considerations: Polling Workaround

While this polling workaround is a pragmatic alternative, it lacks the native capabilities of an event-driven architecture. Review these 7 critical limitations before deploying to production.

1. Polling Latency (Near-Real-Time, Not Real-Time)

  • The Gap: Scheduled runs (e.g., every 10 mins) introduce a maximum data lag equal to the polling interval, whereas an event-driven model pushes changes in seconds.

  • Impact: Field techs may act on stale, modified, or canceled service order data on their mobile apps—a high risk for emergency work orders.

  • Mitigation: Shorten the polling interval during peak hours, balancing against S/4HANA Cloud API rate limits.

2. Snapshot-Only (No Intermediate States)

  • The Gap: Polling only captures a snapshot of the latest state. If an order quickly transitions through multiple statuses between runs (e.g., Released $\rightarrow$ Modified $\rightarrow$ Completed), intermediate states are lost.

  • Impact: FSM business rules triggered by specific state transitions (like ChgdWhenReleased or parts checks) will be skipped, causing workflow inconsistencies.

  • Mitigation: Redesign FSM business rules (if any) to trigger actions based on the final current state rather than historical transitions.

3. Missing ReleaseRevoked Context

  • The Gap: The standard integration publishes a distinct ReleaseRevoked event when a released order is recalled. Polling only detects a raw "Rejected/Revoked" status and cannot determine the historical sequence.

  • Impact: SLA timers or automations meant to cancel upon a revoke action may fail to trigger if the release and revoke both happen within a single polling window.

4. Increased S/4HANA Cloud API Load

  • The Gap: Unlike push events, polling repeatedly queries S/4HANA OData APIs on a fixed schedule, even when no data has changed.

  • Impact: Unnecessary network traffic and rapid consumption of your S/4HANA API license quotas.

  • Mitigation: Implement an adaptive schedule (e.g., poll less frequently overnight/weekends) and routinely monitor API usage logs.

5. Loss of ChgdWhenReleased Granularity

  • The Gap: The standard event model sends precise, field-level delta triggers (e.g., only the schedule time changed). Polling can only see that a change occurred, forcing a full-record refresh to FSM.

  • Impact: FSM automations that depend on specific field triggers (like sending an SMS to a tech only if the priority escalates) cannot be targeted cleanly. FSM will only see a bulk data overwrite.

6. Timestamp-Based Edge Cases

  • The Gap: Delta detection relies strictly on filtering the ServiceDocChangedDateTime field.

  • Impact: Clock drift between CPI and S/4HANA can cause skipped or double-processed records.

    If the CPI local variable storing the Last Run Timestamp is wiped (via redeployment or restart), data will be missed without a manual reset. Boundary records matching the exact timestamp filter might be dropped.

  • Mitigation: Build a 1–2 minute overlap window into your timestamp logic, and set up a monitoring alert for missing or stale timestamp variables.

Conclusion

The absence of SAP Event Mesh is not a roadblock for integrating S/4HANA Cloud service orders with SAP FSM. A custom CPI polling iFlow that mimics an Event Mesh payload offers a viable, non-invasive workaround. By keeping the standard "Replicate Service Order" iFlow completely unmodified, this conservative approach isolates the custom logic into a single, easily maintainable layer.

However, teams must accept the trade-offs: near-real-time latency, the loss of intermediate state history, and added operational complexity around error handling and timestamp management. With a robust retry mechanism and proper monitoring, this architecture can reliably support production workloads.

entry.title: ATUL Architecture #3: Bridging OT and IT: Delivering Mission-Critical Grid Data to SAP BTP Safely, S
entry.content:
ATUL Architecture #3: Bridging OT and IT: Delivering Mission-Critical Grid Data to SAP BTP Safely, Scalably, and Cleanly

1.      Introduction

Utilities are accelerating their digital transformation, but one architectural frontier remains notoriously difficult to conquer:

How do you safely ingest high-frequency Operational Technology (OT) data from substations, feeders, and Intelligent Electronic Devices (IEDs) into SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP) without introducing cyber vulnerabilities or disrupting grid reliability?

Legacy architecture often relied on brittle, custom-coded point-to-point connections or heavy middleware that violated basic security isolation principles. This article provides a comprehensive, production-ready, architecture-driven blueprint for securely integrating:

  • IEC 61850 substation telemetry (GOOSE/MMS)
  • MQTT/Sparkplug B telemetry streams
  • SCADA / RTU / IED asynchronous events
  • Grid-edge IoT sensors

We will achieve this by leverage modern event-driven architectures (EDA), Zero-Trust Network Access (ZTNA), and SAP Clean Core design patterns.

2.      Why OT-to-IT Integration Challenges Enterprise

Bridging the physical grid and the digital cloud requires reconciling two fundamentally opposing engineering philosophies:

Dimension

Operational Technology (OT)

Enterprise Information Technology (IT)

Primary Priority

Availability & Safety: Human life and grid stability. Zero downtime tolerated.

Confidentiality & Integrity: Data security, compliance, and financial accuracy.

Protocols

Industrial, low-overhead, non-IP, or deterministic (IEC 61850, DNP3, Modbus).

Web-native, human-readable, RESTful (HTTPS, OData, gRPC).

Network Philosophy

Air-gapped, strictly segmented (Purdue Model Level 0-3), highly localized.

Cloud-native, perimeterless, distributed, global access.

Data Characteristics

Ultra-high frequency (milliseconds), time-series bursts, massive velocity.

Transactional, structured, stateful, request-response.

To bridge this gap safely, cloud ingestion must be completely outbound-only from the lower levels, strictly audited, cryptographically verified, and decoupled via an enterprise event broker.

3.      Business impact on Utilities

This architecture is not just a technical modernization—it directly enables:

  • Reduced unplanned outages through real-time anomaly detection
  • Lower maintenance costs via predictive asset health insights
  • Improved regulatory compliance with secure audit-ready telemetry flows
  • Faster field response through automated S/4HANA work order generation
  • Scalable grid-edge onboarding without re-platforming legacy OT systems

4.      Reference Architecture: Purdue Model to SAP BTP

The architecture below maps the telemetry flow across the classic Purdue Model for Industrial Control Systems, ensuring that no direct connection is ever established between the cloud and Level 2/3 critical infrastructure.

5.      Architectural Safeguards Highlighted:

  • Directional Isolation: Firewalls block all inbound traffic to the Substation OT network. The Industrial Edge Gateway establishes an outbound connection to the Upper DMZ broker.
  • Decoupling Layer: SAP Advanced Event Mesh (AEM) acts as the shock absorber, ensuring that high-frequency grid telemetry bursts do not overwhelm downstream ERP APIs.

*Architectural Principle: Direct OT-to-cloud integrations without DMZ brokers are inherently unsafe.  Any architecture that bypasses the industrial DMZ violates fundamental Purdue Model isolation and must be avoided.

6.      Deep-Dive: Protocol Translation & Topic Design

 The Conversion: IEC 61850 to Lightweight Cloud Events: IEC 61850 uses Manufacturing Message Specification (MMS) for complex reporting and Generic Object-Oriented Substation Events (GOOSE) for peer-to-peer microsecond trips. These cannot be parsed by cloud apps directly.

An Edge Gateway maps these complex hierarchical Logical Nodes (e.g., MMXU1 for Three-Phase Voltage/Current) into standard JSON structures wrapped in the CloudEvents specification.

Production-Grade Ingestion Payload Example

Below is the exact schema passed from the Upper DMZ to SAP Advanced Event Mesh when a transformer experiences a thermal anomaly:

JSON { "specversion": "1.0",

  "id": "evt-773a-4b92-88ef-22114949ad45", "source": "/us-east/substation-s12/transformer-tx03",   "type":

"com.utility.grid.telemetry.v1",

  "datacontenttype": "application/json",

  "time": "2026-06-01T18:21:55.003Z",

  "data": { "logical_node": "YPTR1",

    "component": "WindingTemperature",

    "metrics": {  "temperature_celsius": 98.4,

      "ambient_celsius": 32.1,

      "cooling_fan_status": "ON_MAX" },

    "status": { "health_score": 72.5,

      "anomaly_detected": true,

      "severity": "WARNING" } } }

Enterprise Topic Hierarchy Best Practices

To optimize routing efficiency within SAP Advanced Event Mesh and avoid bloated subscription wildcards, we enforce a structured, predictable topic hierarchy layout:

$$\text{Domain} \,/\, \text{Business Unit} \,/\, \text{Geographic Zone} \,/\, \text{Substation ID} \,/\, \text{Asset Category} \,/\, \text{Asset ID} \,/\, \text{Event Type}$$

Examples:

  • grid/distribution/northeast/sub-s12/transformer/tx03/telemetry
  • grid/transmission/midwest/sub-s45/circuit-breaker/cb07/state

This allows BTP consumers to subscribe with surgical precision. For instance, a predictive maintenance engine can listen to all transformer telemetry across the entire Northeast region using the pattern: grid/distribution/northeast/+/transformer/+/telemetry.

7.      The Blueprint in Action: A Practitioner Scenario

To understand how this architecture operates under pressure, let's trace a real-world grid event: A severe thermal anomaly on Substation Transformer TX03 located in the Northeast distribution zone.

Step 1: The Edge Trigger (Purdue Level 2)

  1. The physical temperature sensor on Transformer TX03 detects a sudden spike, hitting $98.4^\circ\text{C}$.
  2. The local Intelligent Electronic Device (IED) broadcasts this telemetry via an IEC 61850 MMS (Manufacturing Message Specification) reporting block over the substation's internal fiber optic bus.

Step 2: Protocol Translation & Hardening (Industrial DMZ Level 3.5)

  1. The OT Industrial Edge Gateway (running Litmus Edge) intercepts the raw MMS packet.
  2. It strips out the heavy industrial headers, extracts the data fields from the Logical Node YPTR1 (the standard IEC 61850 node for a power transformer), and maps them into a standardized, web-friendly JSON payload.
  3. The gateway packages this payload inside a standardized CloudEvents v1.0 wrapper.

Step 3: Secure Egress to the DMZ Proxy (Enterprise DMZ Level 3.5)

  1. The Edge Gateway initiates an outbound-only TLS 1.3 connection to the Upper DMZ MQTT Broker (HiveMQ Cluster).
  2. It passes hardware-secured mTLS client certificates to prove its identity and publishes the message to the strict, isolated topic:

 “grid/distribution/northeast/sub-s12/transformer/tx03/telemetry”

Step 4: Ingestion by SAP Advanced Event Mesh (SAP BTP Layer)

  1. The HiveMQ cluster securely routes the incoming stream over a secure WebSocket connection into SAP Advanced Event Mesh (AEM) via Dynamic Message Routing (DMR).
  2. Because AEM natively understands the hierarchical topic layout, it instantly clones and routes the message to three concurrent, decoupled subscribers without any database lag:
    • SAP Datasphere Ingestion Queue: For long-term historical time-series storage and grid analytics.
    • SAP AI Core Engine: To recalculate the transformer's Remaining Useful Life (RUL) score.
    • CAP Event Processor Queue: Dedicated to immediate, critical rule evaluation.

Step 5: Real-Time Orchestration & Clean Core Action

  1. A lightweight SAP CAP (Cloud Application Model) microservice consumes the message from its dedicated AEM queue.
  2. The service executes an automated rule: If temperature_celsius > $95^\circ\text{C}$ and cooling_fan_status == "ON_MAX", trigger emergency field intervention.
  3. Rather than writing complex custom ABAP tables inside the ERP, the CAP service uses the standard SAP Integration Suite to call the out-of-the-box S/4HANA OData v4 API (API_EQUIPMENT_SRV).
  4. The Result: An automated Urgent Corrective Maintenance Work Order is instantly generated in SAP S/4HANA Asset Management with a high-priority dispatch flag—all accomplished within 2.3 seconds of the physical temperature spike, leaving the digital core clean, secure, and upgrade-ready.

8.      Advanced Substation-to-BTP Integration Patterns

 *Reality Check*: Batch ingestion architectures are fundamentally incompatible with modern grid telemetry. Millisecond-level data streams require real-time, event-driven processing models—not delayed batch pipelines.

Depending on your edge compute availability and governance requirements, choose one of these production deployment topologies:

Pattern A: Multi-Tiered Message Broker Architecture (Recommended for Zero-Trust)

  • Mechanism: An Edge Gateway pushes local data to an on-premises DMZ MQTT cluster (e.g., Hive MQ). Secure bridge configuration clones and forwards permitted topics out to SAP Advanced Event Mesh (AEM) via cloud connectors or secure WebSocket’s.
  • Pros: Strict isolation; if the cloud connection drops, the local DMZ broker caches events, mitigating data loss.

Pattern B: Intelligent Edge Compute with Stream Processing (Recommended for High Frequency)

  • Mechanism: Deploy an industrial edge compute node (running lightweight runtimes like Node-RED or KubeEdge) physically inside the substation. It aggregates millisecond telemetry, calculates rolling 1-minute means/standard deviations, and publishes only summarized statistical health events to SAP BTP.
  • Pros: Radically reduces egress data costs and avoids overwhelming BTP with trivial data points.

9.      Security & Governance Blueprint (Non-Negotiable Controls)

Bringing OT data to the cloud is impossible without an airtight security architecture. Implement the following parameters at each layer:

  • Mutual TLS (mTLS) with Hardware Roots of Trust: Every edge gateway must authenticate against the DMZ broker using X.509 client certificates issued by an internal Utility Certificate Authority (CA). Private keys must be stored in secure TPM 2.0 hardware chips on the edge device.
  • Granular Access Control Lists (ACLs): Edge gateways must be explicitly barred from publishing to topics outside their assigned asset scope. A compromise of Substation A must never allow injection of malicious events into Substation B.
  • Schema Validation at the Ingress Gate: Use the Schema Validation features in SAP Advanced Event Mesh. If a message arrives containing bad structures, malformed types, or executable code payloads, it is immediately shunted to a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) for forensics, blocking code injection vectors.
  • Network Partitioning & Backpressure Controls: If the connection between the utility DMZ and SAP BTP degrades, the DMZ broker must utilize Local Storage Buffering. High QoS (Quality of Service) 1 or 2 settings must be applied strictly to critical operational state changes (e.g., breaker trips) to guarantee delivery, while standard continuous metrics use QoS 0 to save bandwidth.

10. Realizing Enterprise Value in SAP BTP

Once normalized grid events stream cleanly into SAP Advanced Event Mesh, they become actionable assets without touching the digital core directly:

*Strategic Insight*: Event Mesh is not optional—it is the control plane for grid-scale ingestion.  Without event-driven decoupling, high-frequency OT telemetry cannot be safely or scalable integrated into enterprise systems.

The Event Consumer Microservices Layer

Deploy lightweight, stateless microservices within the SAP BTP Kyma Runtime or SAP Cloud Application Model (CAP) to process incoming streams:

 

 

 

  • Real-Time Grid Insights: Kyma functions scan the event properties. If a transformer temperature exceeds defined thresholds (temperature_celsius > 95), an immediate event is triggered.
  • AI-Driven Asset Health Optimization: Data streams scale out directly into SAP Datasphere and SAP AI Core. Machine Learning models calculate remaining useful life (RUL) metrics based on historical load/thermal characteristics, sending updated health indices back to operational dashboards.

The Clean Core Imperative

By processing events asynchronously in BTP, the core enterprise system (SAP S/4HANA / IS-U) remains entirely untouched by heavy custom code. S/4HANA only participates when action is required—such as creating an asset maintenance order or executing a field service dispatch via standard standard OData v4 APIs. The system updates and upgrades effortlessly, unencumbered by massive custom databases full of RAW time-series data.

11. End-to-End Flow: Transformer Overheating Scenario

  • A transformer in Substation S12 exceeds thermal threshold (98.4°C).
  • IEC 61850 MMS reports are captured by Edge Gateway.
  • Gateway converts payload to Cloud Events JSON.
  • Event is securely published (mTLS) to DMZ MQTT broker.
  • Broker forwards allowed topics to SAP Advanced Event Mesh.
  • AEM routes the event to a CAP microservice.
  • CAP evaluates rules → triggers anomaly event.
  • SAP AI Core enriches with predictive health score.
  • SAP S/4HANA automatically creates a maintenance work order.
  • Field service team is dispatched proactively.

12. Operational Summary Blueprint

  1. The convergence of OT and IT is no longer optional—it is foundational to modern utilities.
  2. However, success depends not on connectivity alone, but on *how* that connectivity is governed. 
  3. Architectures that prioritize strict isolation, event-driven decoupling, and Clean Core principles will define the next generation of grid intelligence.
  4. SAP BTP, when used correctly, becomes not just an integration platform—but the control tower for real-time, autonomous utility operations.

entry.title: Connection Monitoring: Real-Time Connection Visibility for Event Mesh in SAP Integration Suite
entry.content:
Introduction

When you run a messaging service like SAP Event Mesh in SAP Integration Suite, you quickly accumulate a wide mix of messaging clients and their connections — AMQP-based integrations, MQTT devices, REST publishers, and webhooks. Until now, understanding who is connected, how many connections are active, and which protocols they use meant digging into logs or asking the platform team.

Connection Monitoring changes that. It is now generally available in the Event Mesh in the SAP Integration Suite monitoring UI, as a dedicated screen that provides a real-time, protocol-aware view of all active messaging connections on your service instance.

What is Connection Monitoring in Event Mesh in SAP Integration Suite?

Connection Monitoring provides a live, protocol-aware view of all active messaging connections on a service instance, directly in the Event Mesh in the SAP Integration Suite monitoring UI. You can see which message clients are connected, which protocols they are using, and how that usage has evolved over time.

Key Capabilities

  • Real-time connection overview: A time-series line chart and client table give you an immediate snapshot of all active connections across every message client on the service instance.
  • Protocol-level breakdown: Connections are categorized by protocol — AMQP, MQTT, Webhook, and REST — so you can understand not just whether a client is connected, but how it is connected.
  • Per-client drill-down: Selecting any message client opens a Detail view with a dedicated time-series line chart showing connection details for that client alone, making it easy to isolate anomalies.
  • Chart personalization: Following the SAP Fiori Analytical List Page pattern, the overview provides some standard chart personalization controls — time range selection, zoom, legend selection, and fullscreen mode — letting you tailor the visualization to the window of interest without leaving the screen.

Accessing Connection Monitoring

Step 1: Navigate to Connections in the Event Mesh Monitor

Open your SAP Integration Suite cockpit and navigate to Monitor > Event Mesh > Connections using the left-hand navigation panel.

For official documentation, see Monitor Event Mesh in SAP Integration Suite.

Step 2: Explore the Overview

The main Connections screen presents two components: a time-series line chart at the top and a message client table below. Together, they give you both a historical perspective and a current-state summary of all connections on the service instance.

Connections Per Message Client — chart and client table overview – Analytical List Page Floorplan

The chart is titled Connections Per Message Client and plots the maximum concurrent connections observed per time interval — each message client appears as its own line in the chart. Critically, the chart also displays your tenant's maximum allowed connections and the total concurrent connections across all clients — so you can compare actual usage against your plan limits at a glance. The time range can be adjusted to cover a day, week, or month using the selector in the chart toolbar.

Below the chart, the Message Clients table lists every client on the service instance. The connection counts shown — both total and per-protocol — represent the maximum concurrent connections observed during the selected time range, not a point-in-time snapshot:

  • Message Client Name: The human-readable name as created in your Cloud Foundry environment. If the service instance has been deleted, the client may appear by its GUID instead.
  • Namespace: The namespace the client belongs to, useful for multi-tenant or multi-team environments.
  • Total Connections: The aggregate maximum concurrent connection count across all protocols for that client.
  • AMQP: Maximum concurrent connections using the AMQP 1.0 protocol.
  • MQTT: Maximum concurrent connections using the MQTT protocol.
  • Webhook: Maximum concurrent webhook-based connections.
  • REST: Maximum concurrent connections using the REST messaging protocol.

Step 3: Select a Client to Open the Detail View

Click on any row in the Message Clients table to navigate to the Detail view for that specific client. This is where you go when you need to understand the connection details of one integration in isolation — for example, when troubleshooting a failing integration flow or validating a new deployment.

Connection Monitoring Detail Components

Connections Over Time Chart

The Detail view centers on a chart titled Connections Over Time, which plots connection counts for the selected message client across all protocols that have recorded data. Only protocols with actual connections appear as lines in the chart, keeping the visualization focused and readable. A Max line is also rendered, showing the peak connection count across all protocols at any given point in time.

Connections Over Time — per-client protocol breakdown

The same chart personalization controls available in the Overview are present here: time range selector, zoom, legend selection, and fullscreen mode. Adjusting the time range is particularly useful when correlating a connection drop with a deployment event or an incident window.

Supported Protocols

Connection Monitoring tracks connections across all protocols supported by Event Mesh in SAP Integration Suite. Understanding which protocols a client uses can reveal misconfigurations, unexpected fallback behavior, or opportunities to consolidate connection types.

  • AMQP: Advanced Message Queuing Protocol — commonly used by SAP BTP services and enterprise integration adapters.
  • MQTT: Lightweight publish/subscribe protocol — typical in IoT and high-volume event streaming scenarios.
  • Webhook: Push-based delivery connections — active when Event Mesh is configured to push messages to an HTTP endpoint.
  • REST: HTTP-based messaging — used when consumers or producers interact with queues and topics via REST APIs.

Practical Use Cases

  • Troubleshooting a failing integration: Navigate to the relevant message client and confirm whether an active connection is present. A zero connection count immediately narrows the root cause to the client side rather than the broker.
  • Understanding your integration landscape: The protocol columns in the overview table show you how many connections each client has per protocol, giving you a complete picture of your messaging landscape at a glance.
  • Capacity and scaling decisions: The chart displays a Max VPN Connections line representing your plan's connection ceiling, making it immediately visible when you are approaching the limit. This matters because once the limit is reached, existing sessions continue normally — but new clients cannot connect, and any client that disconnects may be unable to reconnect until usage drops back below the limit.
  • Validating a new deployment: After deploying a new integration flow, open the Detail view for the corresponding message client and confirm the expected connection was established on schedule.

Conclusion

Connection Monitoring closes a significant observability gap for teams operating event-driven integrations on SAP Integration Suite. By surfacing real-time, protocol-aware connection data directly in the monitoring UI — without requiring access to broker logs or external dashboards — it reduces the time needed to diagnose connectivity issues and understand the runtime state of your messaging infrastructure.

If you are interested in complementary visibility tools within Event Mesh in SAP Integration Suite, check out Queue Browser: Deep Message Visibility for Event Mesh in SAP Integration Suite, which covers message-level inspection for queues.

Happy monitoring!

entry.title: ATUL Architecture #4 — AI on SAP BTP for Grid Operations
entry.content:
ATUL Architecture #4 — AI on SAP BTP for Grid Operations

How AI Becomes Actionable Inside SAP Processes

1.      Introduction

Utilities generate massive volumes of operational data every second—from SCADA systems, AMI networks, intelligent electronic devices (IEDs), weather feeds, and grid sensors. While collecting data is no longer the challenge, transforming that data into actionable operational decisions remains difficult. Most AI initiatives stop at dashboards and predictions. However, real business value is realized only when AI insights automatically trigger operational processes inside SAP.

In this architecture, I demonstrate how SAP BTP combines time-series data, machine learning, event-driven integration, and SAP S/4HANA workflows to create a closed-loop operational model where AI does not simply predict problems—it initiates action.

The goal is simple: AI should not just predict. AI should trigger work.

Most utilities already have advanced analytics and dashboards. The real challenge is operationalizing AI—moving from insight to action.
This architecture demonstrates how SAP BTP closes that gap by embedding AI directly into operational workflows, ensuring that predictions automatically trigger governed actions inside SAP S/4HANA.

2.      Foundation: Timeseries + AI on BTP

Time‑Series Data Foundation: Grid operations run on time‑series data. Typical examples include:

  • Transformer temperature curves
  • Voltage fluctuations
  • Feeder imbalance
  • Breaker operation frequency
  • Meter communication patterns
  • Weather impact signals

SAP BTP provides two strong foundations for this:

  • SAP HANA Cloud — native time‑series functions, fast analytics
  • SAP Datasphere — semantic modeling + integration

Most utilities already have this data in SCADA, OMS, or AMI systems. The architecture standardizes and contextualizes this data within SAP BTP, ensuring it is immediately consumable by AI models and downstream processes.

Anomaly Detection on BTP

Once time‑series data is available, the next step is anomaly detection. Common utility scenarios:

  • Sudden voltage drop on a feeder
  • Transformer overheating pattern
  • Meter not reporting for 48 hours
  • Repeated breaker operations
  • Unusual load spike

SAP AI Core + AI Launchpad support models such as:

  • LSTM‑based anomaly detection
  • Isolation Forest
  • Autoencoders
  • Threshold‑based rules for simple cases

The output is always the same: “Something looks wrong here.” But anomaly detection alone does not help operations. The value comes when the anomaly creates an action. In grid operations, the value of anomaly detection lies not in identifying every deviation, but in identifying actionable deviations—those that require operational response within defined time windows.

3.    Predictive Maintenance for Grid Assets

Predictive maintenance models help utilities answer:

  • When will this transformer fail
  • Which feeder is at highest risk next week
  • Which assets need inspection before summer load

SAP BTP supports this through:

  • AI Core for model training
  • HANA Cloud for feature engineering
  • Event Mesh for event‑driven triggers
  • SAP Build Process Automation for workflows

The model output becomes a risk score or failure probability. But prediction alone is not enough. It must flow into SAP S/4HANA. From a business perspective, predictive maintenance shifts operations from reactive repair to risk-based intervention, allowing utilities to prioritize maintenance budgets toward high-impact assets and reduce unplanned outage exposure.

4.    AI Workflow S/4HANA Integration (The "Gatekeeper" Layer)

This is where the architecture ensures both speed and safety. AI becomes valuable only when it creates work, but critical infrastructure requires accountability.

Integrating Manual Approvals: Before the automated creation of a work order in S/4HANA, insert an Approval Step within SAP Build Process Automation.

This “gatekeeper layer” is essential in regulated industries. Fully autonomous AI decisions are rarely acceptable in utility operations. By inserting human approval only when risk thresholds are exceeded, the architecture balances automation with control. This ensures safety, regulatory compliance, and operator trust, while still preserving the speed advantages of AI-driven decisioning.

  • The Pattern: When the AI model reaches a "low-confidence" threshold or identifies a high-risk asset, the workflow automatically pauses.
  • The Interface: A task is pushed to the supervisor's SAP Build Inbox, displaying the AI’s risk score, supporting technical data, and a "Approve/Reject" button.
  • The Result: The S/4HANA work order is only generated after human verification, ensuring that the system is an "AI-assisted" tool rather than a fully autonomous one.
  • AI → Workflow → S/4HANA Integration

This is the most important part of architecture. AI becomes valuable only when it creates work.

Example Flow

  1. AI model detects transformer overheating
  2. Event Mesh publishes an event
  3. SAP Build Process Automation starts a workflow
  4. Workflow checks asset master data in S/4HANA
  5. A maintenance notification or work order is created
  6. Field technician receives the job in SAP FSM or mobile app

This is where utilities see real impact:

  1. Faster response
  2. Fewer outages
  3. Better asset life
  4. Lower O&M cost

AI is not a dashboard. AI is a trigger.

5.    Real Utility Scenarios

Scenario 1 — Feeder Overload Prediction

  1. AI predicts overload 48 hours ahead
  2. Workflow creates a load‑balancing task
  3. S/4HANA logs the action for audit

Scenario 2 — Transformer Failure Risk

  1. Model detects abnormal temperature pattern
  2. Work order created automatically
  3. Technician dispatched before failure

Scenario 3 — Meter Communication Failure

  1. AI detects repeated non‑reporting meters
  2. Workflow assigns investigation to AMI team
  3. S/4HANA tracks resolution

These are simple, but they save real money. Across utilities, such scenarios have the potential to significantly reduce mean time to detection (MTTD), minimize outage duration, and improve asset utilization efficiency.

6.     Architecture View 1: AI‑Triggered Transformer Overheating Workflow (End‑to‑End)

Flow Explanation

  1. SCADA / IoT Gateway Streams transformer temperature every 5 seconds.
  2. SAP BTP – HANA Cloud Stores timeseries + applies smoothing, rolling averages, and feature extraction.
  3. SAP AI Core LSTM model detects abnormal temperature rise → generates anomaly score.
  4. SAP Event Mesh Publishes event: transformer->overheat->detected.
  5. SAP Build Process Automation
    • Reads asset master from S/4
    • Apply business rules (risk threshold, asset criticality)
    • Sends approval task to supervisor
  6. SAP S/4HANA PM
    • Creates Maintenance Notification
    • Converts to Work Order after approval
  7. SAP Field Service Management Dispatches technician with asset details + AI explanation.

7.     Architecture View 2: AMI Meter Non‑Reporting Investigation Workflow

Meter Communication Failure Flow — A simple but high‑value scenario.

Flow Explanation

  1. AMI Headend System Detects meter not reporting for 48 hours.
  2. SAP BTP – Datasphere Harmonizes meter metadata, location, customer info.
  3. SAP AI Core Isolation Forest model identifies “communication anomaly cluster.”
  4. SAP Event Mesh Publishes event: meter->communication->anomaly.
  5. SAP Build Process Automation
  6. Checks if meter is in outage area
  7. Checks last service history
  8. Assigns task to AMI Ops Team
  9. SAP S/4HANA Customer Service / PM Creates service order or investigation ticket.
  10. Technician Mobile App Receives job with meter location + AI reasoning.

 8.    Ground‑Reality Example: “The Black Friday Surge Event”

Black Friday‑style load spikes happen in utilities too — sudden, unpredictable, and dangerous. Here’s the short version you can paste into your paper:

“During a sudden pre‑holiday cold‑weather surge, Feeder F‑19’s load jumped 14% in under 3 minutes. SAP HANA Cloud flagged the abnormal ramp, SAP AI Core predicted an overload within 45 minutes, and Event Mesh triggered an automated workflow. A supervisor approved a pre‑emptive load transfer, and S/4HANA executed the switching plan. The feeder stabilized within 20 minutes — preventing an outage during peak demand.”

9.    Key Architectural Principles

Point 1 “AI runs on BTP, close to SAP data" or AI Proximity to SAP Data Matters

  1. Right now, it just says "No complex integration." That's a feature, not an insight. What you should explain is why proximity matters architecturally — when AI models live in the same platform as your master data, you eliminate the ETL lag, data translation errors, and security surface area that come with external AI platforms. The practical implication: your anomaly detection is working on the same asset hierarchy that S/4HANA uses to create work orders, so there's no mismatch between "what the AI saw" and "what the technician gets dispatched to fix." That's a real architectural win worth spelling out.

Point 2 “Event-Driven Architecture Reduces Operational Latency"

  1. "AI triggers work instantly" is too vague. The deeper idea here is about operational latency — in grid operations, the window between early warning and failure can be hours or even minutes. A polling-based batch integration would miss that window entirely. Event Mesh ensures the moment AI flags an anomaly; the downstream workflow fires. You could contrast this with the old model: AI generates a report overnight, an analyst reviews it in the morning, creates a ticket manually — by which time the transformer has already tripped. Event-driven isn't just faster; it changes the category of what's possible.

Point 3 "S/4HANA becomes the system of action"

  1. The current line misses the real point, which is about organizational trust and auditability. Utilities are regulated industries. Work orders, notifications, and approvals don't just need to happen — they need to be traceable, auditable, and defensible to regulators and internal compliance teams. Because S/4HANA is already the system of record for asset management and maintenance, routing AI-triggered actions through it means you don't need a parallel tracking system. The AI's recommendation and the resulting field action live in the same audit trail. That's not a convenience — it's a compliance requirement for most utilities.

Point 4 “Measurable Business Outcomes Define Success"

  1. "Fewer outages, faster response, better asset health" reads like a brochure. The improvement here is to be specific about how you'd measure these. For example: reduction in mean time to detect (MTTD) on grid anomalies, reduction in unplanned outage minutes per feeder, or improvement in asset utilization rates as preventive maintenance replaces reactive repair. Even if you don't have exact numbers, framing the metrics gives readers a way to build a business case internally — which is often exactly what a utility architect needs when presenting this to leadership.

10.           Governance Considerations

  • AI model versioning and monitoring using SAP AI Core
  • Data lineage and semantic consistency via Datasphere
  • Secure integration through SAP BTP service layer
  • Role-based access for approval workflows

These elements ensure that AI-driven automation remains compliant, auditable, and enterprise-ready.

11.           Final Thoughts

AI for grid operations is not about fancy models. It’s about connecting predictions to SAP processes.

Time‑series data → AI model → Event → Workflow → S/4HANA action.

The future of utility operations is not autonomous AI replacing operators. It is AI-driven workflows that help operators act earlier, with better information, inside trusted SAP business processes. When predictions automatically become notifications, approvals, work orders, and field actions, SAP BTP becomes the operational backbone of grid modernization.

12.           Practical Architecture Example: “The 3 AM Save”

Step‑by‑Step Flow (Real Utility Reality)

  1. 2:58 AM — SCADA temperature spike Transformer T‑221 shows a sudden 9°C rise in 4 minutes.
  2. 3:00 AM — SAP HANA Cloud detects abnormal curve Rolling window + derivative features show a deviation from normal nighttime cooling.
  3. 3:01 AM — SAP AI Core LSTM flags anomaly Risk score jumps from 0.18 → 0.74. Not a failure yet — but trending toward one.
  4. 3:01:10 AM — SAP Event Mesh publishes event grid->transformer->overheat->predicted.
  5. 3:01:12 AM — SAP Build Process Automation starts workflow
    • Pulls asset master from S/4
    • Checks transformer age (17 years)
    • Checks last maintenance (14 months ago)
    • Checks load forecast (high morning peak expected)
  6. 3:01:30 AM — Supervisor approval triggered A mobile notification appears: “AI predicts overheating in 3–5 hours. Approve pre‑failure inspection?”
  7. 3:03 AM — Supervisor taps “Approve” (This is the human‑in‑the‑loop safety layer.)
  8. 3:03:10 AM — SAP S/4HANA creates work order Priority: High Task: Inspect cooling fins + oil level + load tap changer
  9. 3:20 AM — Field technician receives job on mobile Drives to site before failure window.
  10. 4:05 AM — Technician finds blocked cooling fins Dust + debris + vegetation restricting airflow.
  11. 4:40 AM — Issue cleared, temperature stabilizes Transformer returns to normal operating range.
  12. Failure avoided. Outage avoided. $40k avoided. And the entire chain is auditable inside S/4HANA.

What Example Proves (The Architectural Insight)

This single incident captures the entire purpose of architecture. The utility didn’t just detect a problem — it prevented failure because AI, events, workflows, and S/4HANA acted as one system. The model didn’t need to be perfect; it only needed to be early. Event Mesh eliminated latency. Build Process Automation added human judgment. S/4HANA ensured the action was auditable and compliant. And the field technician received the job before the asset crossed the failure threshold.

This is the difference between “AI that predicts” and AI that protects the grid.

entry.title: File to Mesh: Liberating SFTP Data with Micro-Integrations
entry.content:
Introduction

A common integration pattern is to take files from an SFTP server and make their contents available to applications and services through an event-driven architecture. Traditionally, this can involve polling, point-to-point integrations, and additional integration infrastructure.

At the end of last year, Micro-Integrations were introduced as a new capability within SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh. They provide a lightweight alternative for scenarios like this. By bringing integration capabilities closer to Advanced Event Mesh, they can handle simple, high-throughput flows without requiring the full capabilities of Cloud Integration.

In this blog, we will explore the SFTP Source Micro-Integration. It enables you to convert files into JSON messages, publish them to the event mesh, and make them available to your applications at scale in near real-time. From there, the data can be distributed across consuming systems in real time, eliminating the need for complex, polling-based point-to-point integrations.

This blog is structured into five main sections:

  • Introduction
  • The prerequisites
  • The scenario
  • The process
  • Create a 1K broker service in SAP Integration Suite, Advanced Event Mesh
  • Create a temporary SFTP Server
  • Create the SFTP Source Micro-Integration
  • Configure the flow
  • Build the content-based topic
  • Testing the Micro-Integration
  • Troubleshooting
  • Final thoughts

 

The prerequisites

What you need to run through this scenario from A-Z

  1. Make sure you have access to Micro-Integrations.
    If you haven't configured access yet, see Getting started with Micro-Integrations on Advanced Event Mesh: Access Options & Activation first.
  2. Access to SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh, including the required roles:
    1. Mission Control Manager (optional: only in case you don't have a broker yet)
    2. Micro-Integrations Manager
  3. An SFTP client installed on your local workstation.
    In the blog I’m using FileZilla Client, but any equivalent tool should do the job.

The scenario

In this example, a retail chain with stores across EMEA has each point-of-sale (POS) system dropping a CSV file containing sales line items onto an SFTP server, folder:
/upload/retail/sales/inbound.
Every night, a batch job processes these files and loads the data into a data warehouse.

In this process, nothing is broken, but this data is valuable and the way it moves holds it hostage.

It’s not traveling in real-time, so inventory systems can’t react to a sell-out until tomorrow, the store dashboard only reflect yesterday’s data, fraud checks run hours too late, etc.

At the same time, making this data available to additional systems, such as an ERP or loyalty application, requires building new, tightly coupled point-to-point integrations with the SFTP server, increasing complexity and maintenance effort, limiting scalability.

Event-Driven Architectures addresses both challenges, it liberates your data. This doesn’t mean replacing the existing components, it means making the data that is already in the organization available in real-time to whoever (system and applications) needs it by putting a broker between the data source (publisher, SFTP server) and the consuming applications (subscribers).

Whenever a CSV file is updated or a new one is dropped, each line item is converted into a JSON message and published as an event, ready for the subscribers to consume it at their pace.

This approach:

✅  Enables real-time data availability
✅  Decouples producers and consumers
✅  Simplifies and accelerates scaling and onboarding/offboarding of applications
✅  Increases reliability through built-in queueing mechanisms in Advanced Event Mesh

Topic Design

For this scenario, we’ll use for the following topic structure:

retail/sales/lineitem/recorded/v1/{region}/{storeId}/{productCategory}/{transactionId}


Advanced Event Mesh supports dynamically subscriptions using wildcards :

  • *   replaces any string of characters
  • >  matches everything beyond it in the hierarchy.

For example :

  • All recorded sales line items (interesting for ERP, data warehouse and loyalty systems) :
    retail/sales/lineitem/recorded/v1/>
  • Single store dashboard (for store-042):
    retail/sales/lineitem/recorded/v1/emea/store-042/>
  • Product category filtering (e.g. beverages for replenishment):
    retail/sales/lineitem/recorded/v1/*/*/beverages/>

The diagram below highlights how everything is connected :

The process

So, let's get started! 🚀

Create a 1K broker service in SAP Integration Suite, Advanced Event Mesh

Note: if you have already created a broker service, you can skip to step 2 in this section.

  1. Creating the broker
    1. When you open SAP Integration Suite, Advanced Event Mesh, you open what we refer to as the “Cloud Console” (you can always go back to the cloud console by clicking on the SAP logo on the top left).
    2. Navigate to “Mission Control” -> “Cluster Manager”.
       
    3. There you see an overview of your existing brokers, click “Create Service” on the right top.

    4. Provide at least the following 
      • Service Name
      • Cloud provider and region
      • Service Type: Enterprise
      • Service Class: Broker 1K

    5. Click "Create Service"

  2. Once the service is ready:

    1. Navigate to "Try Me!"

    2. Copy the Client Username and Client Password
      ⚠️Important: you will need this later, so you may want to consider pasting this in a notepad.

       

    3.  Click on “Open Broker Manager”, this opens a page where you can publish messages on topic and queues in your broker and subscribe to these messages as well.
    4. Enter your client password in the connect tab and hit connect (on the left side and right side), now you can try out your broker.⚠️ Remember: keep your client username and password at hand!

Create a temporary SFTP Server

  1. Go to sftpcloud.io 
  2. Click on "Create test SFTP Server".
    This creates a test SFTP Server and it is available for one hour. This should be enough for the duration of this tutorial.
  3. After the creation, you see an overview of:
    • Host
    • Port
    • Username
    • Password
      ⚠️Keep this tab open or copy these credentials to a notepad, we will need them very soon.

Create the SFTP Source Micro-Integration

  1. In the Cloud Console, navigate to "Micro-Integrations"

     

  2.  If this is your first time creating a Micro-Integration, you should click on “Get Started with Micro-Integrations”, in the other case just click “Create Micro-Integration” on the right top.

  3. You are now shown a list of different micro-integrations, let’s find the SFTP Source Micro-Integration. Search for “SFTP” using the search bar on the top left and select the “SFTP Source”.

  4. Now, give the Micro-Integration a name and description, for example: 
    1. Name: sftp-retail-source
    2. Description: Liberates batch sales files from SFTP into real-time event stream
      Click "Next".

  5. Enter a name for the checkpoint queue (e.g. ckpt-sftp-retail) and check the box for “Auto Create Checkpoint queue”. The checkpoint queue will keep track of which files and rows have been published, so the process resumes exactly where it left off after a restart or failure.
    Click “Next”
     
  6. Select your broker.

  7. Scroll down and enter the client username and client password of your broker (copied from step 2 in create the broker section).
    Note: for the purpose of this tutorial we’ll leave the rest as-is. For a real use case, you may want to check the authentication settings.
    Click “Next”.

     

  8. At the summary, click on “Create”.

     

Configure the flow

  1. After the creation of the Micro-Integration, you see a pop-up, in this pop-up click on “Create Flow”, this is where the magic happens.

     

  2. Give your flow a name and description, for example:
    Name: sales-csv-to-lineitem-events
    Description:
    Reads each new or updated sales CSV from the SFTP inbound folder, splits it into individual rows, maps every row to a JSON event, and publishes it to retail/sales/lineitem/recorded/v1/{region}/{storeId}/{productCategory}/{transactionId}

  3. Scroll down to “Source Endpoint” and add your SFTP Server URI in the format:

    sftp://<host>:<port>/upload/retail/sales/inbound

  4. Enter the username and password of the SFTP server created in step 2
  5. Scroll down again, and use the following delimiter file configuration:
    • Event delimiter:  \n
    • Field delimiter: ,
      Note: This means that for each line in the CSV file an event will be created, and that fields are separated with a “,”.

  6. Scroll to Target Endpoint and enter the following Topic Name:
    retail/sales/lineitem/recorded/v1
    For our use case, we will work with content-based topics, but since the topic field is mandatory the topic name we add serves as a placeholder.
  7. Click "Next: Error Handling"

  8.  Optionally, you can enable retries and a Dead Message Queue (DMQ) here. Click “Next: Mappings”.

  9. We can now create a mapping, you’ll see a title that says, “No Source Payload”, under this title click on “Import File” and import the Sample JSON.
    After, use the same file for the target payload. We are not going to build a complex mapping in this example, we will focus more on the content-based topics.
    ⚠️Note: Even though we upload CSV files later, the micro-integration automatically converts them to a JSON structure.

  10. After the files are uploaded, link the source and the target fields, they are all the same, make sure you don’t miss one.
     
  11. If you didn’t miss one, you should see a message saying that all target fields are mapped.

Build the content-based topic

  1. Once the mapping is complete, we construct the topic using constants and payload fields. This is how the topic will look like:

    retail/sales/lineitem/recorded/v1/{region}/{storeId}/{productCategory}/{transactionId}

  2. Hoover to the left side of your screen, and click on the “+” button next to “Constants”, under “SFTP Source” and add the following constants:
    • First levels of the topic taxonomy:
      Data Type: String
      Constant Value: retail/sales/lineitem/recorded/v1

    • Separator:
      Data Type: String
      Constant Value: retail/sales/lineitem/recorded/v1

  3. Drag a line from one of the values that we just created to “Smart Topic Destination” and click on “Add transformation”.

  4. Use the Concatenate function and build a transformation that looks this (use “Add input” to add fields):
    • retail/sales/lineitem/recorded/v1
    • /
    • region
    • /
    • storeId
    • /
    • productCategory
    • /
    • transactionId
      ⚠️Ensure there are no double slashes (//) or the topic does not end with a slash (/)
  5. Click "Apply", then click "Next: Summary"
  6. Click "Create".
  7. After a few seconds, a page is shown where you see your Micro-Integration and the flow you just created listed, if you made it this far, click on “Deploy”. A pop-up will show to confirm, confirm by clicking “Deploy” once more.

  8. You should now see that the flow is running successfully.

Testing the Micro-Integration

  1. After you have created the micro-integration, go to the cloud console, go to “Cluster Manager” and open your broker.
  2. Go to the “Try Me!” tab, copy the client password and click on “Open Broker Manager”.

  3. Enter the client password on the left side of the screen and hit “Connect” on both the “Publisher” and “Subscriber” side.
     
  4. Subscribe to topics such as:
    • retail/sales/lineitem/recorded/v1/>
    • retail/sales/lineitem/recorded/v1/emea/store-042/>
    • retail/sales/lineitem/recorded/v1/*/*/beverages/>
  5. Now, go to FileZilla Client (or another File Transfer Client) and connect to your SFTP Server.

  6. You should see the following folder structure: /upload/retail/sales/inbound
    This was created by the Micro-Integration flow we created throughout step 3.
    Note: During the setup of the MI, we specified the folder structure. The moment we deployed the flow, it connected to the SFTP Server and looked for the folders. It didn’t find these folders so it created it.
  7. Click through until you are in the folder “inbound”.
  8. Download the sample CSV.
  9. Upload the CSV into the folder “inbound”.

  10. After the upload, go back to the “Try Me!” tab and, you should see the messages flowing in. Feel free to play around with the file and subscriptions.

Troubleshooting

  1. If issues occur:
    1. Check if the SFTP server is still active (expires after 1 hour)
    2. Verify credentials (broker vs SFTP)
    3. Ensure no // in topic construction
    4. Confirm client permissions on the broker (when you didn’t create the broker from scratch)
  2. You can view logs via: 
    Micro-Integrations -> Select the SFTP Source MI we just created -> 3 dots on top right -> View Error Logs

     

Final thoughts

If everything works like expected, congratulations, you just developed an SFTP source micro-integration!

From here, you can create queues subscribing to the topics used in this example and have various applications consuming from these queues.

Hope you enjoyed this blog!
Curious to hear your thoughts; did you like this blog, are there any other topics you would like me to cover,… feel free to share in the comments!

Event-driven architecture SAP Integration Suite

entry.title: SAP Event Mesh for Beginners – Part 3: Push Delivery with Webhooks
entry.content:
SAP Event Mesh for Beginners – Part 3: Push Delivery with Webhooks

Part 3 of the SAP Event Mesh beginner series.

A quick recap

By the end of Part 2, you had events publishing into Event Mesh over HTTP and CPI consuming them from a queue.

Part 1 (this post):  EDA concepts + provisioning the Event Mesh instance, queues, subscriptions, and service key (https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/sap-event-mesh-for-beginners-part-1-ev...)

Part 2: Testing with Postman + CPI iFlow configuration (publish & consume) (https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/sap-event-mesh-for-beginners-part-2-te...)

Part 3: Push Delivery with Webhooks (https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/sap-event-mesh-for-beginners-part-3-push-delivery-with-webhooks/ba-p/14434605 )
Part 4:  Common errors, fixes, and a quick-reference cheat sheet(https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/sap-event-mesh-for-beginners-part-4-troubleshooting-amp-quick-reference/ba-p/14428993

But there's a catch with everything we've done so far. Every consumption approach in Part 2 was pull-based — your CPI iFlow (AMQP Sender, or the REST /consumption call) reaches out to the queue and asks "any messages for me?" That works, but it means CPI is doing the polling, and there's always a small delay.

There's a second delivery model that flips this around: the webhook. Instead of CPI pulling, Event Mesh pushes — the moment a message lands in the queue, Event Mesh calls your endpoint. No polling, near real-time, and it's the pattern most S/4HANA → CPI integrations actually use in the wild.

If you went looking for "webhook" on the Queue screen and couldn't find it — you're not missing anything. It lives somewhere else, and we'll get there.

 

1. Pull vs Push — when to use which

Both models start the same way: a queue subscribed to your topics collects messages. The difference is who initiates delivery.

  Pull (Part 2) Push (this post)
Who initiatesCPI reaches out to the queueEvent Mesh calls your endpoint
CPI adapterAMQP Sender / REST consumptionHTTPS Sender (receives the call)
TimingPolling intervalNear real-time
Best forBatch-style / CPI-driven pacingEvent-driven, low-latency S/4HANA → CPI

A webhook subscription connects your webhook to a queue, and when messages reach that queue, it delivers them to your webhook in near real time. Because there's no polling, it consumes fewer resources on both sides.

For most "react to an S/4HANA business event" scenarios, push (webhook) is the right choice.

2. Build the receiving iFlow first

A webhook needs somewhere to push to — an HTTPS endpoint that's ready and waiting. In CPI, that's an iFlow with an HTTP Sender adapter. Its address becomes your webhook URL.

  1. Create a new iFlow (e.g. EventMesh_Webhook_Receiver).
  2. On the Sender → HTTPS adapter:
    • Address: something like /eventmesh-webhook → the full URL becomes https://<your-cpi-tenant>/http/eventmesh-webhook
    • Authorization: User Role, role ESBMessaging.send (this is what the webhook's OAuth token will need permission for).
  3. Add whatever processing you need after the sender (map the CloudEvent, call an OData API, etc.).
  4. Deploy the iFlow — the endpoint must be live before you create the webhook, or the handshake (next section) will fail.

 

✅Tip: Copy the deployed endpoint URL from Monitor → Manage Integration Content → your iFlow → Endpoints. That exact URL is what you'll paste as the webhook URL.

3. Get the credential that lets the webhook call into CPI

Here's the single most important thing to understand about webhooks, and where almost everyone gets confused:

⚠️The webhook authenticates INTO CPI — so it uses CPI's inbound credential, not the Event Mesh service key.

Everything up to now used the Event Mesh key (so CPI could talk to Event Mesh). A webhook is the opposite direction: Event Mesh is now the caller, and it needs credentials to get into your CPI endpoint.

Those credentials come from a Process Integration Runtime service instance:

  1. In your CPI subaccount → Instances and Subscriptions → Create → service Process Integration Runtime, plan integration-flow.
  2. Add the role/grant for ESBMessaging.send (API access).
  3. Create a Service Key on it → note the clientid, clientsecret, and tokenurl.

These three values are what secure the webhook. Keep them separate in your head from the Event Mesh key — mixing them up is the #1 webhook failure.

4. Create the webhook

Now the part you couldn't find. It's not on the Queue screen — it's on the message client.

  1. In Event Mesh, open the Overview tab and click your Message Client → this opens the Webhooksconfiguration screen → click Create.
  2. Fill in:
Field Value
Namewebhook-3pl (any name)
Queue NameS4HC/Testing/Masterdata/3pl (the queue to attach to)
Webhook URLhttps://<your-cpi-tenant>/http/eventmesh-webhook (the deployed HTTPS Sender endpoint)
Quality of Service1 (recommended — see section 6)
AuthenticationOAuth2 Client Credentials
Client ID / Secret / Token URLfrom the Process Integration Runtime service key (section 3)
  1. Save. On success you'll see the subscription added.

 

From here, any message that lands in the 3pl queue is pushed to your iFlow — no polling, no AMQP Sender needed.

5. The handshake (what it is, why it fails)

Before Event Mesh sends a single real message, it does a handshake to make sure your endpoint actually agreed to receive pushes.

The handshake is an OPTIONS call to your webhook URL carrying a WebHook-Request-Origin header. Your endpoint must reply with a WebHook-Allowed-Origin header whose value matches that origin (or is *). Only after a successful handshake does Event Mesh start publishing messages to the webhook.

The good news: a properly deployed CPI HTTPS Sender endpoint handles this automatically. The usual reasons a handshake fails:

  • The iFlow isn't deployed or the endpoint isn't reachable.
  • The credentials are wrong (remember: CPI runtime key, not Event Mesh key).
  • The endpoint requires an auth the webhook isn't sending.

If the webhook shows as not active or "handshake failed," check those three before anything else.

6. QoS and the retry behavior

When you create the webhook you pick a Quality of Service:

  • QoS 0 (at most once): Event Mesh posts the message to your webhook and deletes it from the queue regardlessof whether your endpoint succeeded. Fast, but you can lose messages if CPI was down.
  • QoS 1 (at least once): Event Mesh posts the message and waits for a 2XX response as acknowledgment. Any 2XX = success, message removed. Anything else = the message stays and gets retried.

That retry behavior is worth knowing: on a non-2XX response the service resends roughly every 15 minutes, gradually slowing the frequency, and keeps redelivering for up to 30 days unless your webhook positively acknowledges. So a broken downstream won't silently drop events — but it also means a misbehaving endpoint can pile up retries.

✅Tip: For anything you can't afford to lose (master data, business events), use QoS 1. You can pause a webhook during maintenance and resume it later without losing queued messages.

7. Troubleshooting

Symptom Likely cause Fix
Handshake failed / webhook not activeiFlow not deployed, or endpoint unreachableDeploy the iFlow; confirm the endpoint URL from Monitor → Endpoints
401 on deliveryWrong credential direction — used the Event Mesh keyUse the Process Integration Runtime client id/secret/token URL
403 on deliveryOAuth client lacks the API roleGrant ESBMessaging.send to the CPI runtime instance
Messages pile up in the queue, never deliveredEndpoint returns non-2XX (QoS 1 keeps retrying)Fix the receiving iFlow so it returns 2XX; check CPI monitoring
Nothing arrives at allQueue isn't subscribed to the right topic (case-sensitive!)Re-check the queue's topic subscription — same gotcha as the rest of the series

8. Quick Reference

🔒Replace all placeholders with your own values. Never publish real secrets.

Item Value
Where to createEvent Mesh → Overview → Message Client → Webhooks → Create
Webhook URLhttps://<your-cpi-tenant>/http/<iflow-address> (deployed HTTPS Sender endpoint)
Auth typeOAuth2 Client Credentials
Auth sourceProcess Integration Runtime service key (NOT the Event Mesh key)
Required CPI roleESBMessaging.send
HandshakeOPTIONS + WebHook-Request-Origin → reply WebHook-Allowed-Origin (match or *)
QoS 0delete after post, regardless of result
QoS 1needs 2XX ack; retries ~15 min, backs off, up to 30 days
Maintenancepause / resume the webhook

What's next

Webhooks complete the delivery picture: Part 2 gave you the pull model (CPI reaches out), and this post gives you the push model (Event Mesh reaches in). For real-time S/4HANA → CPI event handling, push is usually what you want.

The one idea to carry away: credential direction. Publishing/consuming uses the Event Mesh key; the webhook uses your CPI runtime key, because the caller and callee have swapped.

In Part 4 — Troubleshooting & Quick Reference, we'll bring the whole series together: every error you're likely to hit across setup, publishing, consuming, and webhooks — with causes, fixes, and a one-page cheat sheet to keep open while you build.

🔒Security note: All client IDs, secrets, tenant URLs, and endpoints in this post are placeholders. Use your own values, keep them out of public posts, and rotate anything that's been exposed.
