entry.title: SAP Event Mesh for Beginners – Part 4: Troubleshooting & Quick Reference
entry.content:
SAP Event Mesh for Beginners – Part 4: Troubleshooting & Quick Reference

Part 4 (the finale) of the SAP Event Mesh beginner series.

Part 1 (this post):  EDA concepts + provisioning the Event Mesh instance, queues, subscriptions, and service key (https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/sap-event-mesh-for-beginners-part-1-ev...)

Part 2: Testing with Postman + CPI iFlow configuration (publish & consume) (https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/sap-event-mesh-for-beginners-part-2-te...)

Part 3: Push Delivery with Webhooks (https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/sap-event-mesh-for-beginners-part-3-push-delivery-with-webhooks/ba-p/14434605 )
Part 4:  Common errors, fixes, and a quick-reference cheat sheet(https://community.sap.com/t5/technology-blog-posts-by-members/sap-event-mesh-for-beginners-part-4-troubleshooting-amp-quick-reference/ba-p/14428993

A quick recap

Over the last three posts we set up Event Mesh (Part 1), built the pull-based publish and consume flows in CPI (Part 2), and added webhook push delivery (Part 3). By now you have a fully working, event-driven setup.

But let's be honest about how integration projects actually go: the first time you wire everything up, something breaks. That's not failure — it's the normal path. The difference between a frustrating afternoon and a smooth one is knowing what each error actually means.

So this final post is the one you'll keep open in another tab. Every error below is one I hit (or watched someone hit) setting this up for real. For each: what it looks like, why it happens, and the fix.

 

5. Common Errors & Fixes

The big three (these cost the most time)

invalid_client: Bad credentials (401) — during token request

You enter your client ID and secret correctly, but the token call still fails.

Why: The Event Mesh client ID contains special characters like | and !. When the tool sends your credentials as a Basic Auth header, those characters get corrupted during encoding.

Fix: Send the credentials in the body, not the header.

  • In Postman: Authorization tab → Client Authentication → "Send client credentials in body."
  • In CPI Security Material: this is handled by the Client Authentication setting and, importantly, the Content Type(see the next error).

An Authentication object was not found in the SecurityContext (401) — in CPI

Your iFlow runs, but the publish comes back 401. This message is the resource server (Event Mesh) telling you it received the request with no token at all — which means CPI's token fetch silently failed.

Why (the one that catches everyone): In your CPI OAuth2 Client Credentials material, the Content Type was left as application/json. The XSUAA token endpoint only accepts application/x-www-form-urlencoded for the token call. With JSON, no token is issued, and the request goes out unauthenticated.

Fix:

  1. Security Material → your credential → set Content Type = application/x-www-form-urlencoded.
  2. Confirm Grant Type = Client Credentials (not anything else).
  3. Deploy the credential, then undeploy and re-deploy the iFlow — CPI caches OAuth tokens, so a plain edit won't take effect until you clear that cache.

✅Beginner insight: If Postman works with the same key but CPI doesn't, the problem is always in the CPI credential or the redeploy — never the secret itself. Postman is your source of truth.

amqp:not-allowed (error 220041) — when publishing via AMQP

You point an AMQP adapter at a topic like …/CustomerMaster and get this.

Why: The CPI AMQP adapter lowercases the destination name, so CustomerMaster silently becomes customermaster. That topic doesn't exist / doesn't follow your rules, so Event Mesh rejects it.

Fix: Don't publish over AMQP. Use the HTTP REST adapter to publish (it preserves case). Keep AMQP for consuming, and consume from a Queue (not a Topic) — queue consumption doesn't have the lowercase problem.

The quieter ones (no error, but nothing works)

Publish returns success, but the queue count doesn't move

Everything looks green, but your subscriber queue stays empty.

Why: The topic you published to doesn't exactly match what the queue subscribed to. Topics are case-sensitive, so:

  • …/3PL/CustomerMaster (uppercase) ≠ …/3pl/CustomerMaster (lowercase)
  • …/CustomerMaster ≠ …/customermaster

A message published to a topic nobody subscribed to is simply dropped — no error, no delivery.

Fix: Make the publish topic character-for-character identical to the queue's subscription topic. Check the exact case in the Event Mesh dashboard.

Wrong destination name

You set an AMQP destination like topic:EMISIns/CustomerMaster or some leftover test value.

Why: It doesn't start with your namespace, or it's just not a topic anyone subscribes to.

Fix: Use the real, namespaced topic, with the correct prefix: topic:S4HC/Testing/Masterdata/CustomerMaster.

Webhook errors (push delivery)

Error Root cause Fix
Handshake failed / webhook not activeReceiving iFlow not deployed, or endpoint unreachableDeploy the HTTPS Sender iFlow first; verify the endpoint URL
401 on webhook deliveryWrong credential direction — used the Event Mesh keyUse the Process Integration Runtime key (the webhook calls into CPI)
403 on webhook deliveryOAuth client lacks the API roleGrant ESBMessaging.send to the CPI runtime instance
Messages pile up, never deliveredEndpoint returns non-2XX (QoS 1 retries for 30 days)Fix the receiving iFlow to return 2XX; check CPI monitoring

The URL and connection gotchas

Error Root cause Fix
404 on publish, or wrong routing%2 used instead of %2F for slashes in the topicEvery / inside the topic name must be %2F (the F is required)
405 Method Not AllowedUsing GET on the publish endpointUse POST
404 on /sap-event-mesh/rest/api/v1Wrong management pathCorrect path is /hub/rest/api/v1/management/queues
wss: Name or service not knownAMQP Host field includes a wss://prefix or a typoHost = hostname only, no protocol. Put /protocols/amqp10ws in the Path field
400 Bad Request — WebSocket handshakeAMQP Path empty or wrongSet Path to /protocols/amqp10ws

ℹ️A note for Integration Suite Event Mesh (EMIS) users: If your service key URIs end in …eventmesh.integration.cloud.sap, you're on the embedded EMIS flavor, which differs slightly from standalone Event Mesh:

  • The HTTP REST endpoint uses a specific port :1443.
  • Consuming over HTTP uses /messagingrest/v1/queues/{queueUrlEncoded}/messages/consumption.
  • The OAuth token endpoint is the …authentication.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/oauth/token URL from your uaa block.

6. Key Points Summary

  • Event Mesh follows the Pub-Sub model — part of Event-Driven Architecture (EDA).
  • Topics are channels; queues are mailboxes. One publish fans out to all queues subscribed to that topic.
  • All topic and queue names must start with your configured namespace.
  • Topic names are case-sensitive — CustomerMaster ≠ customermaster, and 3PL ≠ 3pl. This is the #1 cause of "it sent but nothing arrived."
  • URL-encode / as %2F (not %2) in REST topic URLs.
  • For the token request, use Content Type application/x-www-form-urlencoded and send credentials in the body — the |/! in the client ID break Basic Auth.
  • The CPI AMQP adapter lowercases destinations → use HTTP REST to publish, and AMQP + Queue to consume.
  • Pull vs Push: consuming (AMQP/REST) uses the Event Mesh key; a webhook pushes into CPI and uses the CPI runtime key — credential direction flips.
  • A successful publish returns HTTP 204 No Content — no body is correct.
  • CPI caches OAuth tokens — after fixing a credential, undeploy and re-deploy the iFlow.
  • Test in Postman first. If Postman gets a 204 and CPI 401s, the problem is in CPI, not the key.

7. Quick Reference — URLs & Values

🔒Replace <your-subdomain> and all credential placeholders with values from your own service key. Never publish real secrets.

Item Value
Token Endpointhttps://<your-subdomain>.authentication.<region>.hana.ondemand.com/oauth/token
Publish REST URL (standalone)https://<rest-host>/messagingrest/v1/topics/{encoded-topic}/messages
Publish REST URL (EMIS)https://<rest-host>:1443/messagingrest/v1/topics/{encoded-topic}/messages
Consume REST URL (EMIS)https://<rest-host>:1443/messagingrest/v1/queues/{encoded-queue}/messages/consumption
Webhook create pathEvent Mesh → Overview → Message Client → Webhooks → Create
Webhook auth sourceProcess Integration Runtime key (not the Event Mesh key)
AMQP Host<amqp-host> (hostname only — no wss://)
AMQP Port443
AMQP Path/protocols/amqp10ws
Grant Typeclient_credentials
Token Content Type (CPI)application/x-www-form-urlencoded
Client AuthenticationSend credentials in body
Publish headersContent-Type: application/json, x-qos: 0
x-qos0 = at most once · 1 = at least once
Success on publishHTTP 204 No Content

The case-sensitivity checklist (tape this to your monitor):

  1. Does the publish topic match the subscription character-for-character?
  2. Is every / in the URL topic encoded as %2F?
  3. Are you publishing over HTTP (not AMQP)?
  4. Is the credential's Content Type application/x-www-form-urlencoded, and did you re-deploy?

Wrapping up the series

Four posts, one journey: from why Event-Driven Architecture matters (Part 1), through provisioning and the pull-based CPI flows (Part 2), to push delivery with webhooks (Part 3), and finally the gotchas that cost real debugging time (this post).

If you remember only a handful of things, make it these: respect the namespace, respect case sensitivity, encode your slashes, get the token request right (form-urlencoded, credentials in body), and mind the credential direction for webhooks. Nail those and most of the pain disappears.

Thanks for following along the whole way. If this series saved you a few hours, that was the whole point — and I'd love to hear in the comments what you're integrating with Event Mesh.

entry.title: CAP Foundry: Engineering SAP CAP Applications from Business Intent with Guardrailed AI
entry.content:
CAP Foundry is a prototype for engineering SAP Cloud Application Programming Model (CAP) applications from business intent. The user describes the business outcome, selects or supplies the relevant source, and keeps the architecture choices that materially change the application explicit. The Foundry then discovers the source, resolves an application contract, generates a standard CAP Node.js project with SAP Fiori elements, verifies it through executable checks, and delivers it locally or to the SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry environment.

 
Core engineering split: AI helps interpret business intent and business semantics. Verified source evidence constrains the result. Governed generators own repeatable CAP/Fiori construction. Executable checks decide whether the generated application is accepted.
 
Demo video: 

1. Application Requirements as Input

The primary entry mode in the control room is Build from a business requirement. The user does not need to describe files such as schema.cds, service projections, SAP Fiori elements annotations or an MTA descriptor.

A requirement can instead say:

Build a purchase-order application where buyers create and maintain an order with items, validate quantity and price, calculate item amounts, submit and approve the document, publish an approval event, and protect the application with role-based access.

TThe UI still preserves choices that should not be guessed. The user can select or allow discovery to infer the application structure and operation model, choose the business-data source, and choose local CAP runtime or deployment to the SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry environment. The current structures include single entities, associations, parent-child compositions, deeper owned compositions and recursive hierarchies. Operations include read-only, draft-enabled CRUD and analytical read-only.


Business requirement, source and delivery. The application starts from the requested business outcome, a selected business-data source and explicit delivery choices.

2. Discovery Starts With the Source

Business intent is only one input. The second is source evidence. When a real source exists, CAP Foundry inspects that source rather than inventing a model that merely sounds plausible.

Supported source routes include SQLite, an explicitly configured SAP HANA HDI-container source, an existing trusted CAP workspace, offline EDMX, live OData through the SAP BTP Destination service, approved SAP BTP ABAP repository objects, and a bounded two-source application path. For online OData, the control room can inspect metadata and let the user select verified entity sets while keeping destination credentials on the server side.

The ABAP route reads approved repository objects such as tables, CDS definitions and supported read-only program sources through the development tooling boundary. The route has been exercised against an approved SAP BTP ABAP source; as with every live source, a new run still requires valid access to the selected system.

Discovery establishes the facts needed to build the application: relevant objects, fields, keys, relationships, operations, source provenance and enough bounded representative data to understand the selected business shape. It does not treat source discovery as bulk data replication.

Authority rule: source facts and business intent are reconciled before generation. The Foundry does not silently change observed keys, relationships or source capabilities just to make the requirement fit.

3. The Seven-Step Foundry Workflow

The user-facing workflow is deliberately simple:

Intake → Discovery → Build → Verify → Approve → Deliver → Acceptance

Step What the reader should understand

IntakeThe business requirement and explicit choices become a structured application request.
DiscoveryThe selected source is inspected and the supported application shape and capabilities are resolved.
BuildA normal CAP/Fiori project is generated from the validated application contract.
VerifyThe generated project is compiled, built, tested and started; required evidence must pass.
ApproveApproval is bound to the exact reviewed application and evidence.
DeliverThe approved application is run locally or deployed to the selected SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry environment.
AcceptanceThe delivered service and application URL are confirmed.



One completed Foundry run. All seven user-facing stages completed: Intake, Discovery, Build, Verify, Approve, Deliver and Acceptance.

4. What “Guardrailed AI” Means Here

Guardrailed AI is not a claim that the model is somehow prevented from making mistakes. It means the model is placed inside an engineering boundary where its output cannot by itself become accepted application source or bypass the rest of the pipeline.

AI is useful for

  • understanding written business intent;
  • mapping business terminology onto verified source evidence;
  • resolving business semantics that are difficult to express as fixed parsing rules.

Engineering controls own

  • source inspection and provenance;
  • supported structure/capability compatibility;
  • repeatable CAP and Fiori generation;
  • verification, approval and delivery decisions.

The practical consequence is straightforward: an AI response is not a pass condition. If the source cannot support the request, the capability combination is not supported, or the generated application fails verification, the run does not become valid because a model says it looks correct.

Generated projects are also not treated as disposable AI scratchpads. When a reusable generation defect is found, the correction belongs in the Foundry and the application is regenerated.

5. How the Foundry Models Applications

A CAP application is resolved from a small set of architectural dimensions: the business-data shape, the operation model, the source boundary, the capabilities required by the business requirement, and the delivery target.

The current qualification scope covers 19 representative application scenarios across these dimensions. The scenarios are a way to exercise the supported CAP application space consistently; the application itself is still composed from the requirement and verified source evidence.

The application model is compositional:

Dimension Current public-facing choices

Application structureSingle entity, association model, parent-child composition, deep composition, recursive hierarchy
Operation modelRead-only, draft-enabled CRUD, analytical read-only
Source boundarySQLite, configured HANA HDI, trusted existing CAP, offline EDMX, BTP Destination OData, BTP ABAP objects, bounded two-source applications
ConsumerFiori elements by default, with CAP OData service endpoint exposure
DeliveryLocal CAP runtime or SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry environment

Feature richness is applied on top of the compatible structure and operation. Validation, ETags, attachments, events and workflow actions are capabilities of an application rather than separate application types. The 19 qualification scenarios exercise this application space without multiplying every compatible overlay into another scenario.

6. CAP Capabilities the Foundry Can Compose

The capability surface is broader than the handful of applications used in the demo. The table below groups the main capabilities without turning every feature into a separate proof table.

Area Capabilities

Core CAP serviceProjection, filtering, sorting, paging, expand/navigation, read-only OData V4 services and API exposure.
Transactional applicationsFiori draft lifecycle, deep CRUD through owned compositions, declarative validation, rollback, cascade ownership rules and optimistic concurrency with ETags.
Business behaviourCalculated fields, stored determinations, persistent semantic numbering, workflow actions, status transitions and Fiori side effects.
Fiori experienceAnnotation-driven list/object applications, search, localized business text, owned navigation and recursive hierarchy presentation.
AnalyticsOData V4 dimensions/measures, grouping, aggregation, filters, analytical tables and multiple chart presentations when the requirement asks for them.
IntegrationOffline EDMX, live Destination-backed OData, approved ABAP source discovery, external-service delegation and bounded two-source application models.
Event-driven processingTransactional business events, outbox/retry behaviour and configurable broker or queued-service delivery.
DocumentsAttachment upload/download/delete, storage integration and malware scanning integration.
Security & platformService/row authorization contracts, production authentication resources when required, HANA delivery, SAP BTP Destination service connectivity and deployment packaging for the SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry environment.
Temporal dataValidity intervals for compatible writable business objects.

7. Eventing and Attachments Are First-Class Capabilities

Transactional eventing and outbox

A business requirement can ask for an event after a successful business transition. For example, publish an approval event only after an order is actually approved. CAP Foundry can model that event as part of the application contract and generate the CAP-side delivery behaviour with CAP outbox/queued messaging semantics.

The important boundary is transactional: a rolled-back business change must not become a successful external event. Temporary delivery failure can be retried without changing the owning business operation into a second business transaction.

Event delivery is configured at the messaging and deployment boundary rather than embedded as a broker-specific endpoint in the business application. A generated application can use broker-backed messaging or a queued external service, so the eventing route can be selected for the target landscape.

For this implementation, broker-backed delivery was exercised with Solace through CAP messaging. The application still talks to the CAP messaging abstraction; the broker connection and service binding remain environment configuration. That keeps the business event contract independent from the event broker used by a particular deployment.


Solace-backed event delivery. A generated business event is received through the configured messaging landscape while the application remains coupled to the CAP messaging abstraction rather than broker credentials.

Attachments and malware scanning

Attachments are not treated as a decorative upload field. Compatible SAP Fiori elements draft-enabled applications can include upload, download and delete behaviour, storage integration and scan status. For deployment to the SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry environment, the generated deployment can bind object store and malware scanning service bindings so unsafe content can be rejected outside the business-data model.

The demo video shows the user-facing upload and scan-status flow, including a clean scan result.

8. What the Generated Application Looks Like

The result is a conventional CAP project. Depending on the contract, the generated application contains CAP models and services, Node.js handlers where runtime behaviour is needed, SAP Fiori elements annotations and application metadata, generated tests, operational handoff material and deployment artifacts for the SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry environment when cloud delivery is selected.

generated CAP application/
├── db/ CDS domain model and persistence artifacts
├── srv/ CDS service definitions, projections and Node.js handlers
├── app/ SAP Fiori elements applications and annotations
├── test/ Generated behaviour and acceptance tests
├── docs/ Architecture, operations and handover documentation
└── delivery/ SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry deployment artifacts when selected

Repeatable CAP syntax is produced by governed application-generation code and remains tied to the application contract and run evidence.

9. Generation Is Not the Completion Condition

A generated folder is only an intermediate result. Verify independently checks the application using executable CAP and Node.js tooling. The mandatory path covers the areas that matter for a deployable project: model compilation, CAP production build, dependency integrity, clean installation, generated behaviour tests and runtime health. Additional checks are applied when the application uses Fiori, remote sources, security, messaging, attachments or cloud delivery.

The key design rule is that the generator does not mark itself correct and the AI does not mark itself correct.

Executable verification. The run records independent checks for the CAP production build, dependency state, runtime health, artifact integrity, CDS model compilation, supply-chain evidence and generated behaviour tests.

10. Verified Applications

The Foundry was exercised across materially different SAP CAP application patterns. The screenshots below are representative browser-acceptance evidence from generated applications, while the demo video shows the end-to-end flow.

Supplier draft maintenance. SAP Fiori elements draft-enabled maintenance with validation, optimistic locking using ETags, and attachments with upload, download, delete and malware scan status.

Deep sales-order application. Sales Order → Item → Delivery Schedule navigation demonstrates a three-level owned composition exposed through SAP Fiori elements.

Business actions and eventing. The generated application combines draft handling, business actions, side effects and attachment handling. Event publication for the same application flow is exercised through CAP messaging and Solace-backed delivery.

Localization. Generated SAP Fiori elements labels and application texts are rendered in German while the underlying CAP service contract remains unchanged.

SAP HANA-backed delivery analytics. The generated analytical application exposes multiple OData V4 chart views over verified SAP HANA-backed data, together with analytical table and filter support.

Organisation hierarchy. A recursive parent relationship is rendered as an expandable hierarchy while preserving the parent references in the underlying CAP model.

Destination-backed remote application. Remote OData metadata and business data are consumed through the SAP BTP Destination service, with destination credentials kept server-side.

Multi-database maintenance. One draft-enabled CAP application presents data from two explicitly configured database boundaries while preserving the non-atomic failure boundary.

Broker-side event evidence is shown separately in the eventing section because it demonstrates the messaging boundary rather than another SAP Fiori elements presentation type.

11. Local CAP runtime and SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry Environment

Delivery has two current targets: local CAP runtime and SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry environment. SAP Fiori elements applications, OData service endpoints and APIs are outputs of the generated application; they are not separate deployment targets.

Local CAP runtime delivery launches the generated application in a controlled workspace and returns a validated loopback application URL. Deployment to the SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry environment verifies the selected Cloud Foundry org and space, required service bindings, deploys the approved artifact, and then performs acceptance checks against the running application.

Depending on the selected capabilities, the application deployed to the SAP BTP, Cloud Foundry environment can bind the required platform services, including SAP HANA Cloud, authentication and authorization services, SAP BTP Destination service, messaging services, object storage, and malware-scanning services. These are deployment-time service bindings; credentials and secrets remain server-side.

12. What CAP Foundry Does Not Claim

  • It is not a universal CAP generator for every possible CAP/SAP architecture.
  • It does not invent missing source rows, keys, relationships, credentials, roles or business operations.
  • It does not claim one native atomic transaction across independent databases or remote services.
  • The current multi-source read path is intentionally bounded; it is not a general federation/query engine.
  • Remote-service application generation is currently read-oriented.
  • Kyma, SaaS multitenancy and multi-space promotion are outside the current delivery scope.
  • Persistent semantic numbering is not presented as regulated gap-free numbering.
  • Generated application support, automated verification and what is visually shown in the demo are different things; the article does not pretend they are the same evidence layer.

13. Key Takeaways

  • Business intent is the entry point, not CAP syntax.
  • Source evidence remains authoritative. Discovery reads the selected business-data boundary before generation.
  • Guardrailed AI means bounded responsibility. AI helps with meaning; it cannot replace application generation, verification or delivery controls.
  • The product is compositional. Structure, operation, source and capabilities combine into an application contract; 19 qualification scenarios exercise the supported application space.
  • Capabilities go beyond CRUD. Analytics, hierarchy, actions, determinations, ETags, temporal data, eventing/outbox, attachments/scanning, authorization and integration can be composed where compatible.
  • Generation is not success. The application still has to compile, build, test, run and pass the relevant acceptance gates.

Conclusion

CAP Foundry is an engineering prototype for turning business intent and verified data into predictable SAP CAP applications while keeping AI inside a controlled boundary. It can produce materially different applications, transactional SAP Fiori elements maintenance, deep compositions, analytics, hierarchies, remote integrations, event-driven behaviour and bounded multi-source applications without treating every feature as a separate application type.

The useful result is the traceable chain from requirement and source evidence to the generated CAP application, verification and delivered outcome.

This is a prototype and technical demonstration. The supported behavior described here reflects the tested implementation and its current boundaries.

entry.title: The Event & API journey: From S/4 to empowered Agents via Integration Suite/Advanced Event Mesh/MCP
entry.content:
Intro & story

Imagine this: It’s Tuesday, 9:00 AM. The Compliance Manager Michael sets a delivery block on a major Business Partner in SAP S/4HANA due to missing export control documents. Two days later, a million € shipment is ready to leave the warehouse, but the Warehouse Management System rejects it because of the active block. The trucks leave empty. By Friday, the customer TechCorp Logistics is furious, contract penalties are looming, and the Key Account Manager Sarah is still trying to figure out what went wrong.

This is not a fictional nightmare; it’s a classic integration and communication silo problem. But what if we could turn this reactive crisis into a proactive, intelligent, and automated resolution in under 15 seconds?

In this blog post, we will do exactly that. We will build an end-to-end event-driven and AI assisted journey that connects SAP S/4HANA, SAP Advanced Event Mesh (AEM), SAP Cloud Integration (CPI), and an AI Agent powered by SAP AI Core using the latest release of SAP within Integration Suite: The new Integration Cell with SAP APIM and its Model Context Protocol (MCP) Gateway.

 

The Big Picture: Old Way vs. Intelligent reactive Way

Before we dive into the technicalities, let's look at how the paradigm shift looks in practice:

 

The Old Way (Siloed & Reactive)

The New Way (Event-Driven & AI-Assisted)

Trigger

Compliance manager Michael sets a delivery block.

Compliance manager Michael sets a delivery block.

Awareness

Account Manager Sarah has no idea until the shipment fails.

Like a digital nervous system, the solution reacts immediately: Sarah receives an automated alert in her inbox within seconds, notifying her of the delivery block and its consequences for the upcoming high-value delivery.

Investigation

Manually searching through S/4HANA Sales Orders and Business Partner details.

An AI Agent analyzes open orders, assesses financial risk, and drafts a resolution email.

Time to Action

Days (or after escalation).

Proactive: Seconds from save to mail inbox.

 

The Architecture

To make this happen, we will use following hybrid architecture spanning the local Data Center running S/4HANA and the SAP Business AI Platform with Advanced Event Mesh, Cloud Integration and Integration Cell running in the cloud.

 

Here is how the data flows end-to-end:

  1. The Event Trigger: Michael sets the Central Delivery Block.
  2. S/4 Enterprise Event Enablement: SAP S/4HANA fires a BusinessPartner.Changed event immediately.
  3. Event Broker: SAP Advanced Event Mesh (AEM) captures the event and routes and stores it to a guaranteed queue within AEM.
  4. The Orchestrator Cloud Integration:
    1. Event consumption: SAP Cloud Integration (CPI) consumes the event & extracts the Business Partner ID
    2. Fetch BP details: CPI fetches the necessary details on the changed Business Partner from S/4HANA via the API Manager within the Integration Cell runtime.
  5. Guardrailing: CPI evaluates if the BP has a delivery block or if the event was only triggered due to a minor change (like a phone number update). Only if a delivery block is active it invokes the AI Agent.
  6. The AI Brain, MCP Server and smart synthesis: A custom Node.js Agent Loop invokes the S/4HANA Sales Order API—exposed as MCP tools—and interacts with SAP AI Core (hosting Anthropic Claude). The Agent evaluates the open orders, flags high-risk items, drafts a highly contextualized email for the Key Account Manager Sarah, and returns it to CPI.
  7. Automated Dispatch: CPI sends the mail draft straight to Sarah's inbox.
  8. Empowered End User: Sarah can chat with the agent if she has more questions related to the Business Partner or the Sales Orders and clarify with TechCorp Logistics on the next steps.

 

Deep Dive 1: Setting up Event-Driven Triggers in S/4HANA and AEM

The journey begins at the source. Instead of polling SAP S/4HANA for changes, we rely on push-based eventing.

SAP S/4HANA Enterprise Event Enablement

SAP S/4HANA Enterprise Event Enablement is a standard technical framework that enables the publishing and consumption of business events (such as changes to Business Partners or Sales Orders) directly from the ERP backend. It acts as the out-of-the-box bridge that packages these events into standardized formats (like CloudEvents) and securely forwards them to event brokers like SAP Advanced Event Mesh (AEM) to trigger real-time, event-driven processes.

Using the SAP S/4HANA Enterprise Event Enablement framework, we configure an outbound channel binding for the topic space S/4HANA/Events and for this Demo we configure to trigger the
Business Partner Changed Event:

  • ce/sap/s4/beh/businesspartner/v1/BusinessPartner/Changed/v1

SAP Advanced Event Mesh (AEM)

The Advanced Event Mesh is a message broker. Depending on the protocol it listens to or receives Events and (if configured) it stores them in queues to which consumers can subscribe to to receive those events.

Multiple queues can be created and each queue can be configured to receive (subscribe) to different Events (so called topic subscription) as you see in following picture:

For this Demo we configure a dedicated queue to store the business partner changed events named:

  • d/orchestrator/ce/sap/s4/beh/businesspartner/v1/BusinessPartner/Changed/v1

This queue subscribes to the matching Event (topic space + event) from S/4 HANA, ensuring that even if the Orchestrator Consumer (Iflow) is temporarily offline, no business critical event is ever lost (guaranteed delivery):

  • S/4HANA/Events/ce/sap/s4/beh/businesspartner/v1/BusinessPartner/Changed/v1

Once the subscription is configured all business partner events emitted by S/4HANA are stored in the queue. The Orchestrator Iflow  can now connect to the queue and start receiving (consuming) those events.

In the AEM UI it looks like following:

 
Deep Dive 2: API Management & Model Context Protocol (MCP)

After setting up the Events we continue with the API and MCP setup. The API will be used to read additional data on the changed business partner to determine if a delivery block was responsible for the event triggered. The MCP on the other hand is created for the Agent to query open Sales Orders on the changed Business Partner.

API Proxy Configuration via API Manager

Like for the Events S/4HANA also comes with standard APIs out of the box which can be used from external systems to read, write or delete objects such as Business Partners or Sales Orders.

To protect the S/4HANA backend from unwanted or uncontrolled access its recommended to create a layer in front of the S/4 system with API Proxies enhanced with policies meant to gain the necessary control. 

In this Demo we enforce all queries initiated either by the Orchestrator (CPI) or by the AI Agent to go through SAPs API Manager, where we enforce policies such as:

  • Centralized Authorization and Authentication: OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials, Certificates, Scopes, Tokens validation etc.
  • Threat Protection: Active defense against SQL injections, malicious JSON/XML payloads or scripting.
  • Rate Limiting & Throttling: Strict quotas (e.g., 50 calls/min) to prevent AI loops from overwhelming the S/4 system.
  • Semantic Caching: Caching static payloads to minimize load on S/4 and to drastically reduce response times.

Connecting Large Language Models (LLMs) with the MCP Gateway

Connecting Large Language Models (LLMs) to enterprise databases and ERPs has traditionally been a highly customized, messy affair. This is where the Model Context Protocol (MCP) shines.

What is MCP? The "USB-C Port" for AI
Just as USB-C standardized physical hardware connections, MCP standardizes how AI models access data sources, tools, and environments. Developed as an open standard, MCP bridges the gap between LLM knowledge and live, secured enterprise data.

  • Core directives: Provides the AI its job description and rules (e.g. how to behave or how to structure the output)
  • Resources: provides contextual, read-only data sources AI needs to make smarter decisions
  • Tools: Give the AI hands to perform tasks in our systems.  Including the description of tools and how to execute them

In our Demo we create an MCP Server with a registered standard S/4HANA Sales Order API as executable tools (such as get_A_SalesOrder):

When the LLM (Claude via SAP AI Core) realizes it needs context on a specific business partner's open sales orders, it doesn't try to guess or write raw SQL.

Instead it simply checks the registered MCP Server and its schemas and tools provided by the Agent including their descriptions to decide, which tool to call, how to call it and how to formulate/reason the best response.

In our Demo it uses the exposed get_A_SalesOrder tool to fetch all Sales Orders associated with the the Business Partner changed.

 

Deep Dive 3: SAP Cloud Integration (CPI) as the Central Orchestrator

While the AI Agent performs the heavy non-deterministic reasoning, SAP Cloud Integration (CPI) acts as the central deterministic orchestrator which connects all the dots. In short: CPI handles system boundaries and deterministic routing, while the Node.js Control Loop handles iterative LLM reasoning and MCP tool invocation.

  1. Event Consumption: CPI consumes the Business Partner Changed Event.
  2. Extraction: It extracts from the incoming JSON cloud event the BusinessPartnerID.
  3. Enrichment: It calls the S/4HANA API via an API Proxy (/A_BusinessPartner) to fetch the whole Business Partner data.
  4. The Router (Guardrailing): CPI evaluates the returned field DeliveryIsBlockedForCustomer. If the block status is not equal to '04' (or other block codes), the flow ends immediately. This protects the Agent from unnecessary, costly LLM invocations.
  5. Agent Prompt Composition: If the delivery status is detected as '04' a content modifier step dynamically creates a JSON payload specifying the prompt for the agent:
    {
    "question": "List all sales orders for Business Partner ${property.BPId} that are not yet shipped [...] and draft a mailadressed to the key account manager [...]",
    "model": "df9b2e99a335f713",
    "mcpName": "erp-sales-orders"
    }
  6. Agent Call & Cleanup: CPI sends the request via HTTP POST to our Node.js Agent running on BTP. Once the agent loop finishes, CPI cleans up the response and uses the Mail Adapter to route the generated alert mail straight to the responsible Key Account Manager Sarah. She can then clarify with TechCorp Logistics on how to proceed.

 

Demo - and... Action!

Configure S/4 connection to SAP AEM:

 

Set the delivery block on the business partner

 

Check if S/4HANA triggered the Event after BP was changed:

 
 
View the Message Flow in the Orchestrator:
 
 
Mail Alert:
 
 
Interact with the Agent
Ask the Agent on open Sales Orders for a specific Business Partner and if the delivery block is still active

 

Conclusion: Empowering the Enterprise with Event-Driven AI Agents

In this very basic example I showed the role of SAP Integration Suite including Cloud Integration, SAP APIM, SAP MCP and the SAP Advanced Event Mesh in the Agentic AI era:

  • Events keep the system real-time and reactive => nervous system for the autonomous enterprise
  • APIs and MCPs provide secure, governed data access.
  • AI Agents powered by SAP AI Core add contextual reasoning, converting dry technical logs into meaningful, actionable business insights.

A more complex one could include MCP tools to write (not only read) data from S/4 via Agents, multi Agent invocation, invocation of a supervisor agents etc.

The future of enterprise integration is not just about moving data from point A to point B. It’s about building thinking pipelines backed by LLMs with full control on the level on determinism that empower your employees to act before a crisis even hits.

 

Whats next?

SAP has come a long way. Half a decade ago, Enterprise Event Enablement laid the groundwork by event-enabling S/4HANA. In 2022, those capabilities were scaled with SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh. Fast forward to 2026: embedding MCP capabilities into the new Integration Cell runtime together with SAP API Management. Every step brought us to where we are today—powering the potential of Agentic AI.

Yet, this is still not the end. Through the new Developer Hub, SAP provides a central place where APIs, Events, and MCPs can be registered for AI Agents to consume. And despite not all features being available today (like the direct consumption of events) it shows where SAP is heading next. Another one is the AI Gateway scheduled for later this year which I expect to bring LLM guard railing to another level.

And then there is another big topic: Traceability across the systems. Who triggered the event? When was the event triggered? Which Agent reacted on the event? When and how he reacted? Which MCP tools were invoked? Open Telemetry (today already supported by the Advanced Event Mesh) might be the answer to it, but requires all involved systems to support it. Let's cover this in upcoming blog posts! So stay tuned!

How are you planning to integrate Model Context Protocol (MCP) and Event-Driven Architectures into your AI roadmap? Let us know in the comments below!

entry.title: SAP BTP - IS - Beyond the Tool: Frankenstein Landscapes, Art. Sprawl and Integration Storytelling
entry.content:
Knowledge becomes easier to retain when the problem becomes a story.

Teach the problem first. The tool comes later.

Before teaching the tool, make the problem visible.

 

In less than six months, without dedicated budget or corporate support, I produced more than 10 technical articles here in the SAP Community, 30+ articles on other platforms, seven DOI-published specifications representing two architectures DEIP and SDIA, an open-source Kafka adapter, SAP CITS, and the SDIA Control Plane, currently under development.

But producing more was not enough.

I realized that I also needed to improve how I communicate architectural thinking, making complex problems easier for professionals at different levels to understand.

That led me to spend the last three months studying storytelling, visual learning, and scenario-based approaches. The research I reviewed reinforced the direction: narrative formats can improve comprehension and recall.

So this is the new approach I am bringing to the SAP Community: technical problems, development challenges, design decisions, and architecture presented through visual film storytelling first — with the technical depth behind it.

My objective is simple: make knowledge easier to enter, understand, and retain.

Visual Cognition → Abstraction → Perception → Action → Knowledge Sharing → Acknowledgement

The goal is not to reduce technical depth. It is to activate understanding earlier, before the reader reaches the implementation layer.

A Different Way to Learn Integration Architecture

My approach will continue to include written explanations, architecture diagrams, and technical depth. But when the subject allows it, I will also use short narrative films to introduce the problem through an incident, a decision, or a realistic architectural situation.

The objective is simple: create an easier entry point before moving into product-specific terminology and implementation.

The difference is the entry point: story first, implementation later.

Tools change. Architectural problems usually do not.

Frankenstein Landscape - DEIP solves.

A Frankenstein Landscape is not defined by the number of technologies, but by the absence of a coherent architecture above them. 

When platforms, capabilities, ownership, and responsibilities evolve independently, fragmentation follows: teams become tool-centric, governance weakens, and knowledge becomes isolated.

The problem is rarely another tool.
It is the absence of architecture above the tools.

Story Telling Class - Architecture Film of Frankenstein Landscape:

The short film above presents this problem through a storytelling format rather than through a traditional architecture presentation.

From Platform Fragmentation to Artifact Sprawl

Artifact Sprawl happens when integration artifacts grow without clear structure, ownership, traceability, or lifecycle control.

Even technically correct flows, APIs, Packages, Iflows, mappings, credentials, certificates, queues, and runtime resources can become difficult to govern, trace and undeploy retire at scale.

Platform fragmentation can amplify the problem, but even a single platform can suffer from severe sprawl.

The solution is structure, ownership, and governance above the tool.

Artifact Sprawl - SDIA solves.

The next short film looks at the same landscape from another perspective: the organization and governance of the integration artifacts themselves.

Video — Artifact Sprawl

The central question is no longer only which platform contains the integration?

It becomes:

Which domain owns it?

Which capability does it support?

Which other artifacts and runtime resources depend on it?

Who understands it?

And when the integration is no longer required, can we confidently retire everything associated with it?

Those questions become increasingly important as integration landscapes grow.

 Closing

I have tried to bring this content to the highest level of clarity, visual quality, and technical depth I can currently produce.

I have not personally come across many technical articles in the SAP Community using this type of storytelling approach, so I decided to experiment with it.

If this format helps you understand or remember the subject more easily, then it has achieved its purpose. If not, that is perfectly fine as well — people learn in different ways.

There is already content covering HTTPS, SOAP, API Management, TCP/IP, and the OSI model, and the next topic planned for release this week is AMQP, MQTT, and Quality of Service (QoS).

If there is a specific integration or architecture topic you would like to see presented in this format, leave it in the comments. It may become one of the next stories.

And one small disclaimer: please do not ask me for a tutorial on how these films are produced. That part took a considerable amount of time to learn. At the moment, I am the writer, script editor, director, editor, technical reviewer, and everything else in between.

So, no classes on that part. 🙂

Thank you for reading  and for watching.

Ricardo Viana.

entry.title: Part 4: Discover and consume Event APIs from SAP Developer Hub
entry.content:
One of the key benefits of making Event APIs available through SAP Developer Hub is enabling a self-service experience for developers. Whether they are internal developers or external developers and business partners, they can discover Event API Products, subscribe to it, and use the credentials provided by the Developer Hub to consume the events themselves or publish events.

This blog is Part 4 of a four-part series, covering the journey from setting up Advanced Event Mesh to consuming Event APIs through Developer Hub:

  1. Part 1: Enabling Advanced Event Mesh for API Management
  2. Part 2: Connecting Advanced Event Mesh and Developer Hub
  3. Part 3: Publishing event APIs on Developer Hub and managing API Products
  4. Part 4: Discover and consume Event APIs from SAP Developer Hub

You don't need to have followed the previous parts to complete this tutorial. In this part, we’ll take the perspective of a developer using Developer Hub: we’ll discover an Event API Product, subscribe to it, retrieve the required credentials, and use them to connect to the Event Broker and consume events.

We'll cover the following:

  • Before you start (prerequisites):
  • Event API Products: Discover and Subscribe
  • Event APIs: Publishing and Consuming
  • What's next

Before you start (prerequisites):

  1. Be onboarded as an Application Developer in the Developer Hub.
  2. Have access to a client where you can test the connectivity to the Event Broker, in this example I'm using the "Try Me!" in SAP Integration Suite, Advanced Event Mesh
  3. Optionally: Have viewing rights to the Event Portal and Application Domain in your Advanced Event Mesh environment

Event API Products: Discover and Subscribe 

  1. Go to the home page of the Developer Hub and go to your API Product containing event APIs.

     

  2. Under "Events", you see an overview of the event APIs that are part of this product. "Rate Plan" gives you details on the rate plan that is linked to it the event API Product (defines messaging type, access type, queue type, etc.), "Associated Subscriptions" list which applications are subscribed to this Event API Product. Feel free to browse these different tabs.
  3. Now, let's subscribe to the Event API Product, click on the button "Subscribe" on the right top and create the application (either create a new subscription or add it to an existing API application). 

  4. If you're creating a new API Application, enter a name (e.g. Sales Order Application) and optionally a short text and a description and press "Create". 

     

  5. Once you created the application, you will be automatically redirected to the application. Later, you can find the application in the Developer Hub under "My Workspace". 
  6. In the application, you will find the credentials you can use to authenticate to the event broker/event API. "Key" will serve as your username and "Secret" as your password. For this tutorial, copy these credentials. 

     

  7. When consuming events using guaranteed messaging, the application consumes them from a queue. This allows messages to be stored on Advanced Event Mesh if the application is temporarily unavailable or cannot process messages as quickly as they are generated. In this case, you will also need the name of your queue, you find this in your application by going to "Products", select your Event API Product, under "Queue Details" you find the name of your queue. Also copy the name of the queue for this tutorial.

     

  8. Optionally: if you have access to the event portal in Advanced Event Mesh (optional), you will see that after the creation of an application in the Developer Hub a new application is created in your Application Domain.

     

Event APIs: Publishing and Consuming

For publishing events to and/or consuming events from Event APIs using your credentials from the Developer Hub, you can use any client as long as you are able to specifcy the following:

  • Broker URL (e.g.  https://mr-connection-xxxxx.messaging.solace.cloud:9443)
  • Message VPN 
  • Client Username (key copied from Developer Hub)
  • Client Password (secret copied from Developer Hub)
  • Queue Name (name copied from Developer Hub)
  • Topic (found in the Async API spec on the Developer Hub)

Make sure your Queue Name and Topic are in line with the documentation. The key and secret provided are only whitelisted for the topics and queues that are part of the Event API Products in your API Application. If you try to subscribe or publish to a topic that is not included in the API Product, the operation will fail.

⚠️If you don't know which Broker URL or Message VPN should be used, reach out to one of your administrators in SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh.

To demonstrate how the connection works, I will use "Try Me!" in Advanced Event Mesh.

  1. In SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh, go to "Cluster Manager" ➡️ select your Broker Service ➡️ click on "Try Me!" and at the left bottom of the page, hit "Open Broker Manager".
  2. In "Try Me!", enter the following under "Publisher":
    • Broker URL (e.g.  https://mr-connection-xxxxx.messaging.solace.cloud:9443)
    • Message VPN 
    • Client Username (key copied from Developer Hub)
    • Client Password (secret copied from Developer Hub)
  3. Make sure under "Subscriber" you checked "✅ Same as Publisher"
  4. Hit "Connect" at both the "Publisher" as the "Subscriber" side.
  5. You should now see the word "Connected" under "Establish Connections". 

     

  6. Once the connection is established, scroll down to "Bind to an endpoint to receive guaranteed messages" on the "Subscriber" side:
    1. Select "Queue"
    2. Enter the queue name copied from the Developer Hub
    3. Hit "Start Consume"
    4. You should now see that the consumer is active

       

  7. If you were able to subscribe to the queue, scroll down to "Publish to topic" on the "Publisher" side:
    1. Enter the topic you want to publish on (needs to be part of an Event API Product where your API Application is subscribed to)
    2. Delivery Mode can remain "Direct"
    3. Enter a payload under "Message Content"
    4. Hit "Publish"
  8. After publishing events on the topic, you should see the messages appearing on the right side of the page (under "Subscriber"). This means that the messages are successfully being published on the topic and landing in the queue, using the credentials generated by creating an API Application. 

     

What's next 

You’ve now seen how developers can discover, subscribe to, and consume Event APIs through SAP Developer Hub using a self-service approach.

This concludes our journey from setting up Advanced Event Mesh to enabling a self-service experience for developers to consume Event APIs through Developer Hub.

If you want to see the complete picture and how the different pieces fit together, head back to the main blog, which provides an overview of the full series.

entry.title: Part 1: Enabling Advanced Event Mesh for API Management
entry.content:
To bring Event APIs from SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh into the familiar API developer experience of SAP Developer Hub, Advanced Event Mesh first needs to be enabled for API Management.

This blog is Part 1 of a four-part series, covering the journey from setting up Advanced Event Mesh to consuming Event APIs through Developer Hub:

  1. Part 1: Enabling Advanced Event Mesh for API Management
  2. Part 2: Connecting Advanced Event Mesh and Developer Hub
  3. Part 3: Publishing event APIs on Developer Hub and managing API Products
  4. Part 4: Discover and consume Event APIs from SAP Developer Hub

In this first part, we’ll focus on the required setup to enable Advanced Event Mesh for API Management and prepare the environment for the next steps.
Note that in the example we only use 1 broker, if you are using multiple brokers you need to repeat the steps for these brokers as well.

Prerequisites

Before going through this tutorial, we strongly recommend you already have created:

  • a Service in the Cluster Manager
  •  a Modeled Event Mesh in the Runtime Event Manager (containing at least 1 Broker)

The roles required in SAP AEM for this tutorial are:

  • Mission Control Manager
  • Event Portal Administrator 

On your workstation:

  • Terraform CLI Client 
    ℹ️     Don't worry, you don't need any prior Terraform experience.
    That said, some Terraform knowledge can come in handy when troubleshooting. 

Enable Event Broker connections on your event mesh

First, we need to get the endpoint of the broker where you want to enable API connectivity. This is what we'll use in the Runtime Event Manager to enable the connectivity itself.

  1. In the Cloud Console of SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh, go to "Cluster Manager"

     

  2. Go to the the Event Broker where you want to enable API connectivity.

     

  3. Press "Connect", select a Client Library such as "REST", and copy the host
    ⚠️Note: you don't need to copy the protocol (e.g. https) or the port (e.g. 9443), what you copied should be in the following format: ########.messaging.solace.cloud or 123.89.40.72
  4. Once you copied the host, go to "Runtime Event Manager" to enable the connectivity.
  5.  Select the modeled event mesh where you want to enable the API connectivity

     

  6. Click on "Event Broker Connections", select the Event Broker where you want to enable API connectivity and press "View Connection Details"

     

  7. Paste the host under "Host".
    ⚠️make sure you don't have the protocol or port in here!
  8. Add the protocols you need (e.g. REST, SMF, AMQP) by clicking on "Add Protocols".
    You can change transport (e.g. https instead of http) and port settings once you selected your preferred protocol(s).
    For this tutorial I kept the default settings as-is, I just enabled secure transport. The authentication should remain "Basic Authentication".

     

Add predefined client profiles to your Event Broker

Before an Event API Product can be used on an event broker, API Management expects a specific set of six client profiles to already exist on that broker. When an application is approved against a plan, APIM assigns it a client username and picks one of these profiles based on what the plan allows. If the profiles aren't there, that assignment has nothing to point at and application will not work properly.

The six cover the combinations of guaranteed messaging permissions a plan can grant:

Client ProfileGuaranteed Messaging
APIM-NoGMnone - direct messaging only
APIM-ReceiveOnlyGMreceive
APIM-SendOnlyGMsend
APIM-ReceiveSendGMsend + receive
APIM-ReceiveCreateEndpGMreceive + create endpoints
APIM-ReceiveSendCreateEndpGMsend + receive + create endpoints

You could click all six into Broker Manager by hand. But Advanced Event Mesh can be managed via SEMP APIs/Terraform, so let's discover that. There is a Terraform project published on Github that creates the client profiles declaratively, that's what we'll use here. It takes about ten minutes from a standing start, including installing Terraform. More information can be found in the documentation.

  1. Go back to the Event Broker where you want to enable API connectivity (under to "Cluster Manager").

  2. Go to "Connect", go to the bottom and press "SEMP - REST API".
  3. Under "SEMP Credentials", select "Mission Control Manager" (also works with other users as long as it is an admin user), copy the following details and paste it into a notepad:
    • SEMP Public Endpoint (e.g. https://mr-connection-xxxxxx.messaging.solace.cloud:943)
    • Message VPN
    • Username (in this example: mission-control-manager)
    • Password

       


  4. Now, let's use Terraform!
    Open your terminal and to install Homebrew and Terraform, using the following commands one by one (optional, skip if you already have Terraform)
brew tap hashicorp/tap
brew install hashicorp/tap/terraform
terraform -version​

Note: if a Terraform version appears after executing "terraform -version" (e.g. Terraform v1.16.1) the installation of Terraform was successful

  • Use the command line to navigate to the folder where you want to keep the Terraform project (command: cd), and clone the following Git Repository.
git clone https://github.com/solace-cto-labs/terraform-solacebroker-apim-clientprofiles.git
cd terraform-solacebroker-apim-clientprofiles

The project contains 3 files: "providers.tf" names the provider plugin, "variables.tf" contains the inputs, and "main.tf" declares the six client profiles. If you have a look at these files, it is very readable even if you've never seen Terraform.

  • Create a file and name the file "terraform.tfvars", this will contain the values of the variables. This should contain the following:
url          = "https://mr-connection-xxxx.messaging.solace.cloud:943"
msg_vpn_name = "my-service-vpn"
username     = "mgmt-user"​​

⚠️Don't forget to replace the variables in the file with your own url, VPN name and username copied from step 3.

  • Now, go back to the terminal (in folder "terraform-solacebroker-apim-clientprofiles"). In the previous step, we didn't put the password in the file, this we did on purpose. Pass the password as an environment variable using the following command:
export TF_VAR_password='your-management-password'​
  • Let's download the provider plugind:
terraform init​
  • Execute the following command, this reads your broker over SEMP, compares it to the configuration, and prints what it would do without changing anything:
terraform plan​
  • When everything worked fine so far, you can execute the terraform apply command.
terraform apply​

  • It shows the plan again and waits. Type "yes" in full.

  • You should now see that the terraform was applied, for example:
    Apply complete! Resources: 6 added, 0 changed, 0 destroyed.

     
  • You can verify in the cloud console whether the profiles have been added, go to Cluster Manager ➡️ select your Broker ➡️ click on "Open Broker Manager" on the right top.

     

  • Now, go to Access Control ➡️ Client Profiles. You should see the 6 new profiles being listed here.

     

What's next

If you were able to enable the connectivity on your event broker in the Runtime Event Manager and you have added the 6 client profiles: congratulations you have finished part 1 of this blog series and prepared Advanced Event Mesh for integration with API Management.

With this foundation in place, we can now move on to
Part 2: Connecting Advanced Event Mesh and Developer Hub.

entry.title: Part 3: Publishing Event APIs in Developer Hub and Managing API Products
entry.content:
Introduction

With Advanced Event Mesh connected to Developer Hub, we can make our Event APIs available to developers and allow them to subscribe to them.

This blog is Part 3 of a four-part series, covering the journey from setting up Advanced Event Mesh to consuming Event APIs through Developer Hub:

  1. Part 1: Enabling Advanced Event Mesh for API Management
  2. Part 2: Connecting Advanced Event Mesh and Developer Hub
  3. Part 3: Publishing Event APIs in Developer Hub and Managing API Products
  4. Part 4: Discover and consume Event APIs from SAP Developer Hub

In this part, we’ll create and release an Event API in Advanced Event Mesh, publish it as an API Product through Developer Hub, and show you how you can configure that product.

We'll cover the following:

  • Introduction
  • Before you start (prerequisites):
  • Make Event APIs available for Developer Hub
  • Publish an API Product
  • Configure the API Product
  • What's next


Before you start (prerequisites):

  1. Have the Event Portal Administrator role assigned to you in an Advanced Event Mesh instance
    (we’ll be managing Event Portal objects)
  2. Have the “AuthGroup.Content.Admin” role collection assigned to you in subaccount where your SAP Integration Suite tenant is running
  3. Be onboarded as an Application Developer in the Developer Hub.

Make Event APIs available for Developer Hub

In order to make events visible from on the Developer Hub, the event APIs (and all related objects like event and schema) need to be in the “Released” state. If event APIs are not shared, you will still see it in the Developer Hub, but you will not be able to add it to an API Product. Adding an Event API to an API Product is crucial for subscribing to the event API. So, in this part of the tutorial we will make an event API, share it and release it.

  1. Let’s make an Event API, go to Advanced Event Mesh and go to the "Designer".

     

  2. Select the Application Domain where you want to expose the event API from.
    In this example we’ll release a SalesOrder API which is part of the domain “Customer Experience”.

     

  3. Select the table view at left top ➡️ go to “Event APIs” and click “Create Event API”
  4. Enter a name e.g. “Sales Order Events” and enter the following details:
    • Broker Type: Solace
    • Allow Event API to be shared across application domains ➡️ Check ✅!
    • Version Name & Description are optional

       

  5. Scroll down to "Event Flows" and click on “Manage Event APIs”, look for the events you want to make be part of your event API and select whether you want it the API to enable publishing or subscribing (or both) to this event. In this example, I will add all sales order events for both pub and sub.


  6. Once you selected the events, close the “Manage Events” tab and click on “Save Event API” at the right bottom.

     

  7. Now, let’s change the state of the event API to “Released”. In order to do so, all objects related this event need to be in “Released” state. Go back to your event API, click on the 3 dots next to one of the events and click on “Open Event”.

     

  8. Here you’ll see the details of the event, including the schema. If the event schema is not in “Released” state, click on the 3 dots right next to the schema and click on “Open Schema”.

     

  9. In the schema, make sure your version is according to your own guidelines, then click on “Manage Lifecycle”.

     

  10. A pop-up appears, in the drop down box choose “Released” and press “Save”.
    You should see the state of the schema is now “Released”. 

     

  11. Now, go back to your event. Make sure your versioning is according to your own guidelines in the event, click “Manage Lifecycle” as well and also change the state to “Released” and press “Save”.
    In the event, you should now see that both your event and schema are released.

     

  12. Close the tab and repeat this for all events in your event API.
  13. Once all events “Released”, click on “Manage Lifecycle” in your event API and also release the event API. Your event API should look similar to the screenshot below with all events and the event API itself in “Released” state and the Event API Details should mention “Shared”.

     

Publish an API Product

If you have successfully connected the Developer Hub with SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh, you have created an event API and now want to make it discoverable for internal or external developers and allow them to subscribe to the event API, you have to add this an API Product. Before creating an API Product, we will be creating an event rate plan. This rate plan defines the messaging type, access type, queue type, and other configurations that control how events are delivered to consumers. More info on event rate plans can be found in the documentation.

  1. Go to SAP Integration Suite ➡️ Developer Hub ➡️ Admin Center ➡️ Content ➡️ Rate Plans

  2. Under "Rate Plans", click "Create".


  3. Enter a unique name, select a messaging type, access type and queue type and define a maximum time-to-live & spool size and press "Create".

     

  4. Now, we are going to create the Event API Product. Go to "Business Systems", select the SAP AEM Business System we created in Part 2.

     

  5. Click on the Application Domain where you want to expose the event API from (e.g. Customer Experience). Here you should see the event API.


  6. If you click on the event API, you should see the event reference.
  7. Now close the event API.

     

  8. This will take you back to the overview of your event APIs for this application domain. If you select your application domain, you can click on “Create product”.
  9. Enter the product details and hit "Next".
     
  10. Select the rate plan we just created and click "Next".

     

  11. Select the broker where you want to enable deploy the API Product, application and queue to. 
  12. Choose the supported protocols, and click "Next".

  13. Now, you see an overview of the API Product you want to create, if everything looks fine, just click "Publish".

     

  14. A pop-up appears explaining that the request to publish this product has been created. If you want to check the status or finalize the publication of your API product, go to on “Scheduled Requests”.

     

  15. Once published, go to the home page of the Developer Hub, you should see that the API Product has been added.

     

Configure the API Product

  1. In the Developer Hub, go to Admin Center  Content.
  2. Click on “Products” and select your API Product, from here you can edit, unpublish and/or remove the product or alter permissions.

     

What's next

We’ve now released an Event API and published it as an API Product in Developer Hub, making it available for developers to discover and subscribe to.

In Part 4, we’ll complete the journey by subscribing to an Event API from Developer Hub and consuming the events:
Part 4: Consuming Event APIs from SAP Developer Hub

entry.title: Part 2: Connecting Advanced Event Mesh and Developer Hub
entry.content:
With Advanced Event Mesh enabled for API Management (covered in Part 1 of this blog series), we can now connect it to SAP Developer Hub and make the Event APIs available through the familiar developer experience.

This blog is Part 2 of a four-part series, covering the journey from setting up Advanced Event Mesh to consuming Event APIs through Developer Hub:

  1. Part 1: Enabling Advanced Event Mesh for API Management
  2. Part 2: Connecting Advanced Event Mesh and Developer Hub
  3. Part 3: Publishing Event APIs in Developer Hub and Managing API Products
  4. Part 4: Discover and consume Event APIs from SAP Developer Hub

In this part, we’ll create the required API token in Advanced Event Mesh and use it to establish a connection to Developer Hub in SAP Integration Suite.

Before you start (prerequisites):

  1. Have the Administrator role assigned to you in an Advanced Event Mesh instance
    (we’ll be creating a token and managing Event Portal objects)
  2. Have the “AuthGroup.Content.Admin” role collection assigned to you in subaccount where your SAP Integration Suite tenant is running
  3. Have the “Destination Administrator” role collection assigned to you in the subaccount where your SAP Integration Suite tenant is running

Creating an API Token

First, we need to create an API Token in SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh. This API Token will get the right permissions and will be used for authentication by the Developer Hub while connecting to Advanced Event Mesh.

  1. Go to the cloud console of SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh, copy the base URL of your tenant
    (e.g. https://eu20.console.pubsub.em.services.cloud.sap) 
    ⚠️don't forget to copy "https://"
  2. Click on the user icon at the left bottom ➡️ go to “Token Management”
  3. Click on “Create Token”
  4. Enter a name for your token, your API token must have at least the following permissions:
    PermissionsAPI Token Permission
    Allow access to Mission Controlmission_control:access
    Get My Services with Management Credentialsservices:get:self
    Create/Update/Delete Client Profilesservice_requests:post:client_profile
    Get Services with Management Credentialsservices:get
    Read any Applicationapplication:get:*
    Read any Application Domainapplication_domain:get:*
    Do anything to any Event APIevent_api:*:*
    Do anything to any Event API Productevent_api_product:*:*
    Access to Event Portal Designerevent_designer:access
    Get Application Configuration Pushapplication_configuration_push_job:get:*
    Get Environment in Event Portalep_environment:get:*
    Get Event Broker in Event Portalmodeled_event_broker:get:*
    Get Modeled Event Mesh in Event Portalmodeled_event_mesh:get:*
    Create, update, or delete published event API products and their underlaying resourcesapim_event_api_product:*:*
    Get published event API products and their underlaying resourcesapim_event_api_product:get:*
  5. Once the right permissions are selected, click on "Create Token".

     

  6. Now, a pop-up with the API Token appears.
    ⚠️It's is important you copy this token and keep it for the next steps. Once the pop-up is closed you cannot reaccess the API token for security reasons. If you lose it, you’ll have to regenerate the token.

  7. After closing the pop-up, click on the 3 dots at the right side of the token you just created and select “View Token”.

     

  8. Copy the Token ID from the token details.

    ✅If you have the Base URL of your AEM Cloud Console, your API Token and your Token ID at hand you are ready for the next part in this tutorial.

Create a destination on SAP BTP

After creating an API Token in Advanced Event Mesh, we’ll create a destination from the subaccount where the SAP Integration Suite is running. This destination will be used by the Developer Hub to connect to Advanced Event Mesh.

  1. Go to your subaccount ➡️ under “Connectivity”, select “Destinations” ➡️ click on “Create” ➡️ and select “Create New Destination From Scratch”
  2. Give the destination and a name and description and enter the following details:
    • Type: HTTP
    • Proxy Type: Internet
    • URL: [AEM Base URL, copied in step 1 of the previous sections]
    • User: Token ID
    • Password: API Token
    • Additional Properties:
      • Key: sap.isuite.dh.aem.enabled
      • Value: true

         

  3. After you created the destination, you can validate whether everything works fine by clicking on "Check connection" and in Developer Hub. Go to SAP Integration Suite  click on the 9 little dots you see on the right top ➡️ go to “Developer Hub”

     

  4. In the Developer Hub, go to “Admin Center” ➡️ click on “Content”.
  5. Here you should see your Advanced Event Mesh environment under “Business Systems”, the name and description in the table should be the same name and description as your destination. Click on your AEM system.

     

  6. You should see the all your Application Domains being listed. Clicking on the Application Domain, you should see all events available in this domain. If you don’t see any events here, continue this tutorial, it will explain you how to get your Event APIs being published. If you already see some event APIs being there, skip to section "Publish an API Product".
    If you haven't created any Application Domain yet (with applications, schemas and events), please do so, this will be required for the following exercises.

     

What's next

If you see your Application Domains (from AEM) appearing in the Developer Hub it means we’ve now connected Advanced Event Mesh with Developer Hub.

In the next part, we’ll take the next step by publishing Event APIs in Developer Hub and creating and managing the API Products that make them available to developers: 
Part 3: Publishing event APIs on Developer Hub and managing API Products.

entry.title: How to Send Custom RAP Events to Advanced Event Mesh Based on a Custom BOR Object
entry.content:
Custom RAP Events Based on a Custom BOR Object

Overview

SAP S/4HANA's Enterprise Event Enablement (EEE) allows you to publish business events to an event broker such as SAP Advanced Event Mesh (AEM). The standard BusinessPartner.Changed RAP event fires whenever anything on a Business Partner changes — address, bank data, tax numbers, and more. If a downstream consumer only cares about Tax Number changes, subscribing to that broad event means filtering noise, re-reading data via API on every trigger, and handling payloads that contain no Tax Number fields at all.

The approach shown here takes a more targeted path: define a custom RAP event that fires only when a Business Partner Tax Number is created, changed, or deleted, and carries the Tax Number payload directly in the event. No polling, no extra CPI flow, no over-triggering.

Alternative approaches

Before diving in, it is worth knowing that two SAP add-ons can reduce the amount of custom code needed for this kind of scenario:

  • Event Enablement Add-On — ships pre-delivered Function Modules for many standard BOR objects. When the relevant BOR object is covered, the add-on handles the data extraction natively, so the custom Function Module shown in Step 7 would not be needed.
  • AIFAEM (Application Interface Framework + AEM) — the data selection and mapping to the event payload can be configured entirely inside AIF Customizing, without writing ABAP code.

Note that setting up the BOR object behavior is required in all three approaches. The main reason to choose the custom RAP path is a strategic decision to use RAP as the standard event publishing mechanism across your landscape — for example, when you want all outbound events to go through Enterprise Event Enablement with a consistent CloudEvents structure, regardless of whether the underlying data is managed by RAP, BOR, or a classic function group.

This article walks through the full implementation for DFKKBPTAXNUM (Business Partner Tax Numbers). The end-to-end flow looks like this:

Tax Number changes in S/4HANA
        │
        ▼
Change Document written to CDPOS (MKK_BPTAX)
        │
        ▼
BOR event TAXNUMBERCHANGED fired (SWO1 / SWEC / SWE2)
        │
        ▼
Function Module ZAEM_RAP_EVENT_HANDLER called
        │
        ▼
Reads current data → calls ZBP_R_BPTAXNUMBER=>raise_changed / raise_deleted
        │
        ▼
RAISE ENTITY EVENT in RAP behavior saver
        │
        ▼
Event published via Event Binding (Z_BPTAXNUM) to AEM_BROKER

Step 1 – Create the RAP Data Model Objects

You need two CDS artifacts: a root view entity that acts as the RAP business object, and an abstract entity that describes the event payload.

Root View Entity – ZR_BPTAXNUMBER

The root view entity selects from the API CDS view A_BusinessPartnerTaxNumber. The two key fields are BusinessPartner and BPTaxType.

CDS@AccessControl.authorizationCheck: #NOT_REQUIRED
@EndUserText.label: 'BP Tax Number - Root View Entity'
@Metadata.allowExtensions: true

define root view entity ZR_BPTAXNUMBER
  as select from A_BusinessPartnerTaxNumber
{
  key BusinessPartner,
  key BPTaxType,
      BPTaxNumber,
      BPTaxLongNumber,
      AuthorizationGroup
}

 

Abstract Entity – Z_BPTAXNUM_EVT_PAYLOAD

The abstract entity defines the structure of the event payload. The @event.context annotation tells EEE which field to use as a dynamic topic segment — here xsaptaxtype.

CDS@EndUserText.label: 'BP Tax Number Event Payload'
define abstract entity Z_BPTAXNUM_EVT_PAYLOAD
{
  @Event.context: { attribute: 'xsaptaxtype', position: 1 }
  TaxType            : abap.char(4);
  BPTaxNumber        : stcd1;
  BPTaxLongNumber    : abap.char(60);
  AuthorizationGroup : abap.char(4);
}

 

Step 2 – Define the Behavior and the Implementation Class

Behavior Definition – ZR_BPTAXNUMBER

The behavior definition declares three events (Created, Changed, Deleted), all using the abstract entity as payload type. Because the RAP object is only used for event publishing — not for CRUD operations — it uses an unmanaged save implementation.

ABAPmanaged with unmanaged save implementation in class ZBP_R_BPTAXNUMBER unique;
strict;

define behavior for ZR_BPTAXNUMBER
  lock master
  authorization master ( instance )
{
  event Created parameter Z_BPTAXNUM_EVT_PAYLOAD;
  event Changed parameter Z_BPTAXNUM_EVT_PAYLOAD;
  event Deleted parameter Z_BPTAXNUM_EVT_PAYLOAD;
}

 

Implementation Class – ZBP_R_BPTAXNUMBER

The generated behavior pool class ZBP_R_BPTAXNUMBER exposes three static raise_* methods. Each method delegates to a local event-handler class (lcl_event_handler) that issues the actual RAISE ENTITY EVENT statement.

ABAPCLASS ZBP_R_BPTAXNUMBER DEFINITION
  PUBLIC ABSTRACT FINAL
  FOR BEHAVIOR OF ZR_BPTAXNUMBER.

  TYPES tt_created TYPE TABLE FOR EVENT ZR_BPTAXNUMBER~Created.
  TYPES tt_changed TYPE TABLE FOR EVENT ZR_BPTAXNUMBER~Changed.
  TYPES tt_deleted TYPE TABLE FOR EVENT ZR_BPTAXNUMBER~Deleted.

  PUBLIC SECTION.
    CLASS-METHODS raise_created IMPORTING it_events TYPE tt_created.
    CLASS-METHODS raise_changed IMPORTING it_events TYPE tt_changed.
    CLASS-METHODS raise_deleted IMPORTING it_events TYPE tt_deleted.
ENDCLASS.
